The Complainant requests the Commission to: a) Grant provisional measures to the family of the victim; b) Consider a transfer of the Communication to the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights pursuant to Rule 118(3) of the Rules of Procedure of the African Commission, the case being one of the many cases of serious human rights violations, notably extrajudicial executions, committed during that period; c) Declare the present Communication admissible; d) Find that the facts disclose a violation by the State Party with respect to the Late Juvénal Havyarimana of Articles 2, 4, 5, 6, 9(2) and 10 read together with Article 1 of the African Charter; e) Order Burundi, pursuant to Articles 7(1)(a) and 26 of the African Charter, to conduct a prompt, thorough and effective investigation into the execution of the First victim and the other violations suffered, by independent and impartial judicial bodies, with a view to instituting criminal proceedings against the perpetrators and punishing them; f) Require Burundi to immediately suspend administratively the alleged perpetrators pending the institution of proceedings; g) Order Burundi to provide appropriate reparation to the beneficiaries of the First victim, including measures of financial compensation for the material and non-material harm caused, restitution, psychological, social and economic rehabilitation and satisfaction. Require Burundi to provide guarantees of non-repetition, in particular through public apologies addressed to the relatives of the First victim and a strong message condemning such acts and their impunity; h) Request Burundi to urgently adopt legislation aimed at protecting victims and witnesses, notably in the case of judicial proceedings, in order to effectively guarantee the right of access to courts; i) Request Burundi to adopt all necessary measures to ensure that such acts do not recur and to ensure political pluralism; j) Request Burundi to publish the findings of the African Commission; k) Order Burundi to report, within 3 months, on the action it has taken on the conclusions of the African Commission.

The Complaint reached the Secretariat of the African Commission by email of 19 February 2016. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 4 March 2016. It also informed the Complainant that there was confusion in the documents transmitted on behalf of this Communication. The Complainant responded to the request for clarification by email of 9 March 2016.

On 23 March 2016, the Secretariat received by post all the documents relating to the complaint. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 24 March 2016 and asked the Complainant to provide an indication regarding the time limit provided for the submission of Communications. The Complainant responded by email of 4 April 2016 and the Secretariat acknowledged receipt by letter of 12 April 2016.
At its 58th Ordinary Session held from 6 to 20 April 2016, the African Commission considered the Communication and decided to be seized of it.

By letter dated 5 May 2016, the Secretariat transmitted the decision on seizure to the Complainant and requested him to submit his observations on the admissibility of the Communication within two (2) months from notification. By Note Verbale of the same date, the Secretariat transmitted the decision on seizure and the Communication to the Respondent State.

Regarding the provisional measures requested by the Complainant, the Commission did not grant them on account of the incomplete and, above all, imprecise information provided to it for the examination of the need for such a measure.

At its 20th Extraordinary Session held from 9 to 18 June 2016 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission decided to defer its decision on admissibility since it was awaiting the Complainant's observations on the said admissibility. On 27 June 2016, the Secretariat of the Commission notified the parties of this decision.

By letters of 29 June 2016 and 4 July 2016 respectively, the Complainant indicated that he maintains the arguments and evidence on admissibility contained in his initial submissions and that there is no new element to bring to the attention of the Commission. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt of both correspondences on 1 September 2016.

On 1 September 2016, the Secretariat retransmitted the Complainant's initial submissions to the Respondent State and invited it to submit a brief on admissibility within two months from receipt of the request in accordance with the provisions of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

On 24 November 2016, the Secretariat notified the Respondent State of the decision to grant it an additional 30 calendar days for the submission of its observations on admissibility. The notification of this decision was also sent to the Complainant on the same date.

At its successive sessions, the Commission noted the absence of submission of the Respondent State's observations on admissibility within the time limit. The Secretariat notified the Parties of the consecutive deferrals of the Commission's decision on the admissibility of the communication. Reminders were sent to the Respondent State by Note Verbale.

At its 61st Ordinary Session held from 1 to 15 November 2017 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Communication and deferred it for the preparation of a decision on the basis of the information in its possession, given that the Respondent State had not submitted its brief on Admissibility despite the multiple reminder Notes Verbales.

The Commission took note of the Complainant's request for referral of the case to the Court. Although the Complainant is recognised as having the right to make requests, notably a request for referral of the case to the Court, the Commission considers that once it is seized by the Complainant, the latter recognises its competence to decide on the Communication. The Commission recalls that the referral of a Communication falls within its discretionary power and that it may exercise it if and whenever it deems it necessary. In the present case, the Commission does not deem it necessary to refer the case to the Court.
Consequently, the Commission decided not to grant this request
The Complainant argues that the Communication meets the admissibility requirements set out in Article 56 of the African Charter.

The complaint presents the identity of the authors of the Communication. The Communication concerns Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana and the family of the victim, represented before the Commission by the non-governmental organisation Track Impunity Always (TRIAL) whose address and contact details are clearly specified in the submissions.

The Complainant asserts that the Communication is compatible with the Charter of the OAU/AU or with the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights pursuant to Article 56(2) of the Charter. According to the Complainant, the present Communication is directed against the Republic of Burundi, a State Party to the Charter since 30 November 1989. He also alleges the violation of the rights guaranteed by Articles 1, 2, 4, 6, 9(2) and 10(1), and 18(1) with respect to the victim subsequent to the ratification of the Charter by the Respondent State.
The Complainant declares that no other international body has already ruled on the matter in accordance with the requirement set out in Article 56(7) of the Charter.

On the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies, the Complainant raises a precedent in which the African Commission admitted and developed exceptions to this principle. According to the Complainant, the Commission considered that this requirement "should not constitute an unjustifiable impediment to access to international remedies", it being understood that it must be applied in connection with Article 7 of the Charter. The Complainant puts forward three main reasons preventing him from complying with this fundamental requirement.

Firstly, the Complainant argues that the existing local remedies were pursued in order to obtain justice, and that they were prolonged in an abnormal manner. In support of such an allegation, the Complainant recalls that the facts date from 28 May 2012, that upon the discovery of the victim's body, judicial authorities including the Prosecutor of "Mwaro" and a Judicial Police Officer of "Nyabihanga" (OPJ), were informed and even rushed to the scene. According to the complaint, an investigation was purportedly opened on an unspecified date by the judicial authorities. According to the Complainants, the investigation of the file relating to the murder of the victim continued until March 2013 (Confer para 14). However, 3 years and 7 months have elapsed without any follow-up and the facts remain unpunished, the Complainant stresses.

Secondly, the Complainant asserts that the remedies proved ineffective and unsatisfactory. According to the Complainant, the attempt by the victim's family to obtain information on the file under investigation, to provide additional information and even to join the proceedings as a civil party were in vain. According to the complaint, the victim's family was neither summoned in the context of an investigation, nor called to any hearing. The complaint adds that the family was neither informed, nor called as a civil party at the first public hearing scheduled in the context of the trial against the person named "Rwembe". The Complainants assert that no information was given to them regarding the progress of the said investigation despite the mobilisation of non-governmental organisations on behalf of the victim's relatives for a prompt and effective investigation with a view to prosecuting the alleged perpetrators.

Thirdly, the Complainant puts forward that it is dangerous to use local remedies. The complaint relies on a precedent between The Gambia and one of its nationals, a case in which the Commission specified that, if the complainant could not have recourse to the courts of his country for fear for his life or that of members of his family, the said remedies are considered non-existent for him. In this vein, the Complainant presents the context that followed the discovery of the victim's body, based on growing pressure, exacerbated threats, and creating an environment of fear for the family.

With regard to the victim, the complaint states that this context of insecurity led to his dropping out of school and his change of residence in order to protect himself against death threats. Likewise, the complaint supports such a position not only by an arrest of the victim, without any basis, but also by the resignation of a police officer fearing for his life after having been questioned about the death of the victim.

Moreover, with regard to the non-governmental organisations that denounced this murder and demanded a prompt investigation, the radio affiliated with the ruling party accused the human rights defenders not only of wanting the overthrow of legitimate institutions but compared them to enemies of the Republic, the complaint states. This same radio called on the Burundian population to attack the three leaders who, according to it, were seeking to destroy the works of the population and sabotage the celebration of the fiftieth anniversary of independence, the complaint mentions. The complaint asserts that this call endangered the lives of these three personalities. The existing witnesses are increasingly reluctant for fear for their safety in such a context corroborated by the absence of a legal and institutional framework to ensure the safety of witnesses and victims, the complaint mentions.

The Complainant asserts that the communication was submitted within a reasonable time in accordance with Article 56(6). In support of such an allegation, the Complainant states that the communication could not have been submitted to the African Commission earlier for two reasons.

Firstly, the notion of induced prolongation of time limits must take into consideration the chronic failings of the judicial system in Burundi. According to the Complainant, such failings are reflected in the weakness and slowness of investigations and widespread impunity, corroborated by the near-dependence of the judiciary on the executive, elements regularly pointed out by the international community, including United Nations bodies and international non-governmental organisations (NGOs). The Complainant notes in a jurisprudential precedent that the obligation to exhaust local remedies not only makes it possible to make known to the State the existence of a human rights violation but also to give it the opportunity to remedy it before any seizure of an international mechanism. The Complainant asserts that in the present case, the existing local remedies were pursued in order to obtain justice, but they were prolonged in an abnormal manner and proved futile and ineffective. In the view of the African Commission, this induced prolongation must be interpreted in the light of the "circumstances of the case, the context, the political situation in the country, the judicial history of the country, as well as the nature of the complaint". According to the Complainant, the communication could not be submitted before the procedure could be described as unduly prolonged, better still without a real opportunity having been given to the State to remedy the violations perpetrated, in this case, an appropriate time before seizing an international mechanism at the risk of being seen as "impetuous".

Secondly, the Complainant considers that the advocacy of NGOs and the actions of United Nations bodies offered concrete opportunities to the State to remedy the violations. In view of the specificities of justice in Burundi, victims of serious human rights violations often have no other choice but to rely on advocacy actions for years, the Complainant states. Furthermore, the Complainant puts forward a resolution of the United Nations Security Council underlining "the need to conduct thorough, credible, impartial and transparent investigations into these serious crimes, in particular extrajudicial executions, and calls upon the Burundian authorities to put an end to these criminal acts and to ensure that their perpetrators are brought to justice." To this the Complainant adds the recommendations made to the Burundian authorities by the United Nations Human Rights Council in January 2013 as well as the concerns of States regarding extrajudicial executions and the prevailing impunity, requiring serious investigations and the said perpetrators to be brought to justice.

The Complainant reaffirms that the communication was submitted within a reasonable time, that in this regard, the general human rights situation, which has deteriorated drastically since December 2015, must also be considered, highlighting inter alia several hundred allegations of torture or ill-treatment, thousands of persons arbitrarily detained, hundreds of persons killed and forced migrations to neighbouring countries. Such a context objectively makes it more unlikely that the Burundian State would take up a case that it had not previously taken up. The Complainant argues that the victim's family cannot obtain redress before the national courts, which is why it decided to turn to international justice.

Lastly, the complaint therefore stresses that the victim's family, from a modest and disadvantaged background, could not promptly and effectively seize an international human rights protection body, and that prior knowledge of the existence of such a body is necessary before accessing free legal assistance. In "a concern for equity and justice", the condition of the victim's family cannot prevent the individual communication concerning Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana from being examined by the African Commission, the Complainant recalls. It is therefore appropriate to take into consideration the concrete opportunity of access to international bodies in the present case. The Commission is therefore respectfully requested to declare the individual communication admissible.

The Respondent State did not submit its observations on Admissibility despite the multiple reminder Notes Verbales that the Secretariat sent to it for that purpose; notably the Notes Verbales bearing the references ACHPR/COMM/607/16/BUR/1481/16, ACHPR/COMM/607/16/BUR/1872/16, ACHPR/COMM/607/16/BUR/265/17, ACHPR/COMM/607/16/BUR/399/17, ACHPR/COMM/607/16/BUR/684/17 and ACHPR/COMM/607/16/BUR/1582/17 of 1 September 2016, 24 November 2016, 13 April 2017, 5 June 2017, 22 August 2017 and 8 December 2017 respectively.
Article 56 of the African Charter prescribes seven (7) conditions that must be cumulatively fulfilled for a Communication to be declared admissible by the Commission.

The Commission notes that despite the multiple requests addressed to the Respondent State to obtain its arguments on admissibility in the communication at hand, in accordance with Rule 102(2) of its Rules of Procedure, it has not responded.

In several of its previous decisions, the Commission has established that in the absence of a substantive response from the Respondent State, it decides on the basis of the facts communicated by the Complainant.

The Commission notes that the Complainant has submitted arguments on all the criteria required by Article 56 of the African Charter. It observes that in the present case, only the conditions provided for in paragraphs (5) and (6) of Article 56 on the exhaustion of local remedies, and the time limit for submission of the Communication to the Commission could be contested by the Respondent State.
Turning to the admissibility conditions set out in Article 56 of the African Charter, the Commission will first address those on which there is no disagreement between the parties.

The Commission considers that the Communication fulfils the condition set out in Article 56(1) in that the identity of the author is clearly indicated. Indeed, the Communication is submitted by Track Impunity Always (TRIAL) on behalf of the Late Juvénal Havyarimana and his family against the Republic of Burundi, a State Party to the African Charter, and the Complainant has standing.

As regards Article 56(2), the Commission notes that the Complainant alleges the violation of the African Charter, notably Articles 1, 2, 4, 6, 9(2) and 10(1), and 18(1) with respect to the victim. The Commission further notes that the Charter was in force in Burundi at the time of the facts. Finally, it is manifest that neither the claims nor the requests contained in the Communication infringe any of the principles adopted under the Constitutive Act of the African Union. Consequently, the Commission concludes that the Communication complies with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter.

On compliance with the provisions of Article 56(3), the Commission finds that the Communication does not contain any term that could be described as insulting or disparaging towards the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union. The Communication therefore fulfils the condition under examination.

The Commission also notes that the requirement of Article 56(4) is met since the Communication is not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media but also on testimonies, extracts of reports of non-governmental organisations, extracts of reports of international organisations such as the United Nations.

As regards Article 56(7), the Complainant has indicated that the issues raised in the Communication have not been settled by another international body. The Commission therefore considers that this requirement is fulfilled.

Concerning Article 56(1) of the Charter, the Commission finds that the Complainant has provided his identity as well as that of the victim. The Commission declares itself satisfied that the five (5) conditions provided for in Articles 56(1), (2), (3), (4) and (7) are fulfilled. It will rule on the status of the condition in Article 56(6) in the light of the conclusions of the analysis of Article 56(5).

As a prelude to the analysis relating to Article 56(5), "Communications must be submitted after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious to the Commission that the procedure of achieving these remedies would be unduly prolonged". In its jurisprudence, the Commission has considered that three major criteria must be met in determining the exhaustion of local remedies, which must be available, effective and sufficient, also observing that "a remedy is considered available if the petitioner can pursue it without impediment, it is deemed effective if it offers a prospect of success and it is found sufficient if it is capable of redressing the complaint". Where one of these characteristics is not met, the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies is deemed not to have been satisfied as stipulated in Article 56(5).
In the present Communication, the Complainant argues that local remedies were unduly prolonged, that they proved ineffective and unsatisfactory and that their exhaustion represents a danger.

The Complainant submits that the victim's sister attempted to lodge a complaint and to join the proceedings as a civil party, but that no action was taken on her request. Indeed, the victim's body was discovered on 28 May 2012, and when the facts occurred, the Prosecutor of Mwaro ordered the judicial police officer of Nyabihanga to do "what is necessary to shed light on this case and to transmit the file to the Prosecutor's Office of Gitega". Moreover, according to the authorities, an investigation was reportedly opened in June 2012. However, 3 years and 7 months later, no action has been taken on this case.

He further adds that the notion of undue prolongation has not been precisely circumscribed by the Commission, but that the jurisprudence it has developed on this subject provides indications on this issue. Indeed, in its Communication 293/04 - Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa v. Zimbabwe, the Commission affirmed the need to take into consideration the circumstances of the case and the reasons put forward to justify the prolongation of remedies in order to determine whether the prolongation is normal or abnormal.

The Commission notes that the Complainant has demonstrated his willingness to seek justice and it is confirmed that an investigation was opened but that it remained at a standstill until its seizure. It also notes that similar cases of extrajudicial execution involving in particular the alleged perpetrator of the murder of the victim benefited from more speed, up to the holding of a first public hearing. Furthermore, as submitted by the Complainant, nothing justified this accumulated delay in the handling of the victim's file, given that the judicial institutions were operational and able to function normally throughout this period.

Consequently, the slowness of the investigation truly constitutes an obstacle to the effective administration of justice and it can therefore be considered that there is an undue prolongation of the procedure, consequently the Commission decides to uphold the Complainant on this ground.

The Commission has, in its jurisprudence, indicated that a remedy that has no chance of success does not constitute an effective remedy and that a remedy is satisfactory when it is capable of giving satisfaction to the Complainant and of redressing the alleged violation.

In the present case, it emerges from the information submitted by the Complainant that the authorities at various levels (political, judicial, municipal) were informed of the facts, which gave rise to the opening of a judicial investigation at the Prosecutor's Office of Mwaro. However, until the date of the seizure of the Commission by the Complainant, no information concerning the progress of the investigation was available. Likewise, no member of the victim's family was heard on the matter.

The Commission also notes that the Respondent State limited itself to initiating a judicial investigation relating to the discovery of the victim's body, whereas the Burundian Code of Criminal Procedure understands by investigation: "all the acts whose object is to search for the perpetrators of offences, to gather evidence and to take measures intended to enable the courts to rule with full knowledge of the facts".

In the Communication SERAC v. Nigeria, the Commission had concluded that remedies were ineffective following the inaction of the Respondent State despite the fact that it had been amply informed of the alleged violations. More pertinently, in the Communication Article 19 v. Eritrea, it had considered that faced with the inaction of the Respondent State, one can consider either that local remedies do not exist, or, if they exist, that they are ineffective [...].

The Commission considers that the Complainant has amply demonstrated his willingness to exhaust local remedies, but that, the conclusions of the investigation that should allow the indictment of the alleged perpetrator(s) still not being available, the remedies have been unduly prolonged. In the absence of arguments from the Respondent State that could justify this slowness, the Commission considers that the remedy is ineffective.

Moreover, it is commonly accepted that for a remedy to be effective it must present all the guarantees making it possible to obtain the solution sought or at least to guarantee with certainty convincing prospects capable of giving satisfaction. In the present case, the local remedies being ineffective and presenting no plausibility of resolving the problem, they cannot be considered satisfactory.

As regards the dangerous nature of local remedies, the Commission has considered that "if the complainant cannot turn to the court of his country because he fears for his life or that of members of his family, local remedies are considered non-existent for him". Such a consideration presupposes a fear justified by the context and circumstances surrounding the case giving rise to the violation.

The Complainant recalled the climate of insecurity that led to the murder of the victim and the threats to which he was subjected before his death. Moreover, the status of the alleged perpetrator, who holds the rank of Deputy Commissioner of the Gitega police, also represents a ground for fear, in a context where allegations of extrajudicial executions involving State agents rarely reach a judicial outcome. Furthermore, following the discovery of the victim's body, the said Deputy Commissioner had visited the victim's sister at her home and following this visit a Gitega police officer, a former friend of the victim, had reported to her that this Commissioner was the murderer of her brother. The Complainant states that this police officer gave up his duties because he feared for his life.

The Commission considers that if local remedies prove dangerous for the Complainant, it would not be reasonable to ask him to exhaust them. After analysis of the Complainant's arguments it is evident that there is a high risk in making use of local remedies and in the absence of elements contradicting these arguments, the Commission decides to uphold the Complainant on this point.

Finally, as regards the condition prescribed by Article 56(6) of the African Charter according to which the Communication must "be submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized of the matter". The Commission having already established the fact that the remedies are unduly prolonged, it is appropriate to confirm whether the time limits of submission meet its criteria.

Unlike the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and the American Convention on Human Rights, which set a specific time limit of six months for the submission of communications, the African Charter only provides that communications must be submitted "within a reasonable period", which is not defined.

In its Communication Michael Majuru v. Zimbabwe, the Commission had considered that "six months seems to be the usual standard", but that "each case must be treated on its own merits" and thus, "where there are valid and compelling reasons why the complainant could not submit his complaint in time, the Commission may examine the complaint in order to ensure equity and justice"

In the present case, the Commission notes that the facts date back to 4 June 2012 and the related communication was received on 19 February 2016. In order to justify the delay that could be considered late by the Commission, the Complainant stresses the need to be convinced of the undue prolongation of local remedies, the context that prevailed during the Burundian crisis of 2015, the modest condition of the family and its lack of knowledge of the existence of the Commission.

Having already clarified that no period from which the prolongation may be considered abnormal is expressly retained, and having regard to the modest condition of the family, to which is added its ignorance of the existence of the Commission before having received the Complainant's assistance, the Commission considers, as it recalled in its Communication Darfur and Documentation centre v. Sudan, that it is its responsibility to offer the Complainant the opportunity to be heard in a concern for equity and justice, where there are valid and relevant reasons that justified the delay.

On the basis of the aforementioned facts and following its jurisprudence, it appears to the Commission that the time within which it was seized can be considered reasonable and upholds the Complainant on this ground.

In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights: (i) Declares the present Communication admissible in accordance with Article 56 of the African Charter; (ii) Defers the examination of the Communication to allow the Parties to present their observations on the merits, in accordance with Rule 107(2) of its Rules of Procedure; and (iii) Requests the Complainants to submit their observations on the merits within sixty (60) days from the date of notification, in accordance with Rule 108(1) of its Rules of Procedure.

The Complainant alleges that the facts described in the present communication constitute violations with respect to Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana of Articles 2, 4, 5, 6, 9(2) and 10(1) read together with Article 1 of the African Charter. A violation of Articles 5, 7(1)(a), 18(1) and 26 read together with Article 1 is also alleged with respect to the victim's family.

Under Article 2 of the African Charter, "[e]very individual shall be entitled to the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms recognized and guaranteed in the present Charter without distinction of any kind such as ... political or any other opinion"

In the present case, the Complainant states that Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana suffered an infringement of his freedom of opinion, expression, assembly and association because of his membership of the MSD party and his political commitment, notably as a member of the "Youth of the MSD party in Gitega" committee.

Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana was an active member of the said opposition party and, during the 2010 elections, he had actively participated in the campaign for the said MSD. It was following the electoral period that the victim began to receive death threats, suggesting to him that he had very little time left to live. The victim expressly reported to his sister that the threats came notably from the Imbonerakure, the youth of the ruling party, and were motivated by his political affiliation.

Indeed, as mentioned previously, supporters and members of opposition parties, including the MSD, were particularly targeted by serious human rights violations during the post-electoral period. They suffered restrictions on their rights because of their involvement in an opposition party. In 2011, the BNUB and the High Commissioner for Human Rights recorded further human rights violations, including 61 cases of extrajudicial, arbitrary or summary executions and/or political assassinations, most of the victims being affiliated with a political party. Often the alleged perpetrators of these crimes belonged to the security or defence forces.

In this respect, Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana, clearly identified by the authorities and the Imbonerakure as an active member of the MSD, suffered discrimination based on a prohibited ground which resulted in irreversible violations of his rights.

According to Article 4 of the African Charter, "Human beings are inviolable. Every human being shall be entitled to respect for his life and the integrity of his person. No one may be arbitrarily deprived of this right."

In the present case, Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana suffered a violation of his right to life. He was indeed found dead on 4 June 2012 on Munago hill, in the commune of Nyabihanga. The criminal nature of the victim's death is beyond doubt and is moreover confirmed by several elements. Notably, the doctor who was at the place where the body was discovered, Doctor Melchior, after examining the body, stated that the victim had been strangled. Moreover, in the presence of witnesses, the Prosecutor of Mwaro ordered the Judicial Police Officer of Nyabihanga, Mr. Révérien Ntakirutimana, to do what was necessary to shed light on this case and to transmit the file to the Prosecutor's Office of Gitega. Finally, according to the information gathered by the CNIDH, the Prosecutor's Office of Gitega allegedly opened an investigation file on this matter and a file was also allegedly investigated by the Prosecutor's Office of Mwaro.

It must be noted that this violation of the right to life was inflicted on the victim outside any judicial proceedings against him. Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana was indeed killed after being abducted by people in police uniform and taken away in a double-cabin vehicle. No trial was held. In this respect, this violation must be characterised as extrajudicial.

Moreover, it is firmly argued that agents of the Burundian State were involved in this violation of the right to life. In the first place, the person who had contacted Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana on the evening of the abduction inviting him to leave the house was a person who had been visiting the victim at his cousin's for some time, pretending to be a member of the FNL. In fact, after the death of Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana, it was discovered that this person worked under the orders of Mr. Michel Nurweze, alias Rwenbe, the Deputy Commissioner of the Gitega police. In the second place, according to the witnesses of the abduction, the victim was abducted by people in police uniform. In the third place, a Gitega police officer, called Willy, a friend of the victim, reported to Ms. Imelda Niyonzima that the Deputy Commissioner of the police in Gitega was responsible for the murder of Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana.

The victim had reported that the threats came notably from the Imbonerakure, the youth of the ruling party. Yet, it has been established that the members of the youth league of the CNDD-FDD act in concert with and/or with the consent of State authorities. In numerous testimonies, the Imbonerakure beat people in the presence of police officers who remain passive. In other testimonies, the violence is committed both by the police and the Imbonerakure acting in concert.

In its concluding observations of 2014, the Committee against Torture expressed concern about "the serious human rights violations perpetrated by a group of youths close to the authorities called Imbonerakure, such as the harassment of political opponents, the disruption of public meetings, O intimidation, arbitrary arrests and detentions, and even the use of violent acts and the resort to settling matters 'amicably'".

The general context of harassment going as far as the execution of other political opponents by State agents, widely documented and denounced, constitutes an additional indication allowing the conclusion that the State was involved in this case.

Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana having suffered a violation of the right to life caused by State agents or with their consent outside the framework of a trial, it must be found that he was the subject of an extrajudicial execution.

The State also violated the obligation to investigate the facts, which are nevertheless of particular gravity. Indeed, although a judicial file was opened, no investigation was ever conducted. The judicial authorities did not show effective guarantees of impartiality and independence in this case. The victim's family was never heard. No result was ever communicated either to the family or to the NGOs mobilised. The facts remain unpunished and the victim's family has never received reparation.

The State also did not take all the necessary measures to prevent such an act and to protect Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana. In view of the number of cases of extrajudicial executions of political opponents documented over this period, it can be found that the State failed in its general obligation to prevent such acts and to protect its nationals.

Under Article 5 of the Charter, "Every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited."

In the present case, Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana was the victim of an extrajudicial execution between the time of his abduction - 28 May 2012 - and the time the body was discovered - 2 June 2012. He was thus removed from the protection of the law and suffered an irreparable violation of his life and his physical and psychological integrity. In this respect, he was denied in the very essence of his person, which implies a violation of his dignity and his legal personality.

In the present case, the members of the victim's family were plunged into immense suffering following the loss of their relative in such a violent and brutal manner. His sister, Ms. Imelda Niyonzima, stated that the death of her brother has left a void: "He is irreplaceable." Their father, a widower, will never recover from it. Furthermore, the uncertainty that prevails as to the circumstances of the victim's death and the absence of identification of those responsible is a source of deep suffering for the family. Indeed, the absence of an effective investigation into the facts to shed light on them sustains the anguish felt. This feeling is further exacerbated by the fact that, according to the victim's sister, witnesses exist and they were never heard.

Article 6 of the African Charter provides that "[e]very individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained.

In the present case, Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana suffered several violations of his liberty and security. As regards his security, he was first of all the subject of death threats by the Imbonerakure, because of his political affiliation with the MSD. Yet, as we have argued above, these persons act in concert with or with the consent of State agents (see supra, paras. 236-237).

Moreover, the abduction of Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana constituted an arbitrary deprivation of liberty, in that it took place outside the framework of the law and in violation of the rules provided for by both domestic and international law, without charge or bringing the victim before a court. As explained previously, in view of the continuous harassment by the Imbonerakure to which the victim was subjected before being found dead, the fact that the victim was abducted by people in police uniform and that the person who made him leave the house in order to be abducted was a person working under the orders of the Deputy Commissioner of the Gitega police, it is firmly argued that the abduction and the execution that followed are the work of State agents. The general context of harassment going as far as the execution of other political opponents by State agents, widely documented and denounced, constitutes an additional indication allowing the conclusion that the State was involved in this case. Furthermore, this abduction led to the execution of the victim and thereby constitutes a violation of his security. The State failed in its obligation to protect the victim against abuses by public authorities.

Under Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter, "[e]very individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force;

In the present case, the matter was the subject of broad mobilisation by NGOs which demanded the opening of a thorough and independent investigation aimed at the prosecution and punishment of the perpetrators as well as reparation for the victim's family. Among others, the APRODH immediately informed all relevant authorities and the matter was publicly denounced by public figures. Although a judicial file was apparently opened, no effective and complete investigation was conducted. It therefore appears that local remedies were pursued, in vain however, because they proved ineffective and unsatisfactory (see also supra for all details, section 3.2.2.). It is evident that the Burundian authorities were not unaware that such a crime had been committed against Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana and on that basis, they should have taken all necessary measures to shed light on the facts. It must be concluded, however, that despite the steps initiated, the cause was not heard.

Furthermore, as has been amply demonstrated in paragraphs 165 et seq. of the present communication, cases of extrajudicial executions remain largely unpunished in Burundi. The Burundian judicial system suffers from significant dysfunctions, including the lack of independence from the executive power, which today represents a major obstacle to the fight against impunity for these crimes. The victim's family was therefore prevented in practice from accessing an independent court.
Under Article 9(2) of the African Charter, "Every individual shall have the right to express and disseminate his opinions within the law."

In the present case, Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana stood out because of his political opinions and the expression of these through his active involvement in the MSD, as demonstrated by paragraphs 217 to 221 possibly establishing the causal link between his membership of an opposition political party and his possible extrajudicial execution.
Under Article 10(1) of the African Charter, "Every individual shall have the right to free association provided that he abides by the law."

In the present case the persecution and execution of Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana because of his membership of an opposition party constitutes a violation of the freedom of association protected under Article 10(1).

Under Article 18(1) of the African Charter, "The family shall be the natural unit and basis of society. It shall be protected by the State which shall take care of its physical health and moral." In the present case, the execution of Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana entailed a break-up of the family unit and a violation of the psychological health of the members of the family, notably his sister and his father, who is moreover a widower. They were plunged into acute suffering following his death, all the more so as the circumstances surrounding it are particularly violent and have not been clarified since. The fact that those responsible have not been clearly identified and in particular have not been prosecuted further exacerbates their suffering.

A testimony of the victim's sister, in despair at the void left by his absence, was reported in a press article of November 2013: "His sister, Ms. Imelda, still in shock, states that the death of their brother has left a void: 'He is irreplaceable.' Their father, a widower, will never recover from it. Imelda explains that after the announcement of the judgment rendered against Rwembe, she fainted: 'Especially as witnesses exist.' However, she believes that as the days go by, the witnesses become more reluctant because they fear for their safety: 'How can one dare to accuse someone supported from the bottom to the top of the institutions?'"

The principle of equality, set out in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the African Charter, stipulates that all individuals are born free and equal, without distinction of race, colour, gender, language, religion, political opinions, nationality, social background, property or birth. Discrimination based on other grounds may also be considered unlawful. Direct discrimination occurs when a person is treated less favourably because of his political convictions or activities, while indirect discrimination arises when regulations or policies appear to grant equal treatment, but in reality, certain individuals are treated less advantageously because of specific characteristics. The African Commission has established its position on political discrimination, notably in the case of allegiance to an opposition party.

In Andrew Barclay Meldrum v. Zimbabwe, the Commission defined discrimination as "any act of distinction, exclusion, restriction or preference based on any of the grounds listed in Article 2 of the Charter and which has the purpose or effect of nullifying or impairing the recognition, enjoyment or exercise by all persons, on an equal footing, of all rights and freedoms".

The African Commission clearly listed the conditions required to determine a violation of the principle of non-discrimination in Kenneth Good v. Republic of Botswana. Thus, the violation can be found if: a) similar cases are treated differently, b) the difference in treatment does not have a reasonable objective and justification and c) there is no proportionality between the aim sought and the means employed. These conditions have been expressly set out by international human rights monitoring bodies, such as the European Court of Human Rights, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights and the Human Rights Committee.

The principle of non-discrimination extends the protection of the African Charter, in particular on the basis of political opinions, thus, in the case of Amnesty International v. Zambia, the Commission considered that Article 2 places an "obligation on the Government to secure the right protected in the African Charter to all persons within its jurisdiction, irrespective of political or other opinion".

In the present case, during the 2010 elections, Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana had actively participated in the campaign for the said MSD. It was following the electoral period that the victim began to receive death threats, suggesting to him that he had very little time left to live. According to the testimonies of his sister, the threats came notably from the Imbonerakure, the youth of the ruling party. As a result, Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana had been clearly identified by the authorities and the Imbonerakure as an active member of the MSD.

In 2011, the BNUB and the High Commissioner for Human Rights recorded further human rights violations, including 61 cases of extrajudicial, arbitrary or summary executions and/or political assassinations, most of the victims being affiliated with a political party. Moreover, supporters and members of opposition parties, including the MSD, were particularly targeted by serious human rights violations during the post-electoral period.

Individuals must be equally protected by the law, regardless of their political convictions. However, in this case, it is clear that the victim was persecuted because of his affiliation with an opposition party, which led to acts of violence and even to an extrajudicial execution of him. The facts indicate that the State did not protect the victim because of his political activities. The actions of the agents being clearly biased and based on political discrimination, the Commission concludes that there is a violation of Article 2 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights and the principles for failure to protect an individual because of his political convictions.

The right to life falls within the category of human rights, which are intrinsic and inalienable rights, inherent in all human beings. Every human being enjoys all the other rights stipulated and guaranteed by the constitution and international documents by virtue of the right to life. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights stipulates that everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person (Article 3).

In the case of Noah Kazingachire, John Chitsenga, Elias Chemvura and Batanai Hadzisi (represented by Zimbabwe Human Rights NGO Forum) v. Zimbabwe, the Commission held that international human rights law requires the State to respect and ensure the right to life and that it has the obligation to prevent the wrongful death of its citizens. It must ensure that its organs respect the life of persons under its jurisdiction.

It emerges from the Complainant's statements and the documents produced in the procedural file that Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana was found dead on 4 June 2012 on Munago hill, in the commune of Nyabihanga, after having been abducted by people in police uniform and taken away in a double-cabin vehicle. The doctor who was at the place where the body was discovered, Doctor Melchior, after examining the body, stated that the victim had been foreign and reported that the victim had been contacted by an individual who worked under the orders of Mr. Michel Nurweze, alias Rwenbe, the Deputy Commissioner of the Gitega police, information which was confirmed by the testimony of Ms. Imelda Niyonzima, who stated that she had seen the Deputy Commissioner of the police in Gitega and that he was therefore responsible for the murder of Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana.
In this regard, given the testimonies indicating that the victim was in the hands of State agents, the Commission establishes that the right under Article 4 has been violated.

Article 5 of the Charter stipulates that every individual has the right to respect for his inherent dignity and to the recognition of his legal personality, prohibiting all forms of exploitation and abuse, such as slavery, trafficking in persons and torture. Dignity is now considered an attribute inherent in all human beings, and human rights aim to guarantee the protections flowing from this dignity. The recognition of legal personality is crucial because it enables each individual to participate fully in social life and to access all his rights. The jurisprudence clearly underlines what constitutes a violation of human dignity, notably the disrespect of one's honour and worth, as well as the denial of access to one's fundamental rights.

Consequently, it is thus that the Commission has highlighted actions that inflict severe physical or psychological suffering and that humiliate the individual as being a violation of the right to dignity, Spilg and Mack & DITSHWANELO (on behalf of Lehlohonolo Bernard Kobedi) v. Botswana and Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and Interights v. Egypt.

The Commission has further established that the violation of dignity through torture corresponds to severe punishments or suffering, caused by or at the instigation of a public authority for the purpose of punishing or obtaining information or confessions. These punishments or sufferings may be physical or mental.
Furthermore, the Commission also considers that Article 5 prohibits any act that humiliates the individual or compels him to act against his will or conscience.

Article 5 of the African Charter explicitly prohibits torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, adopting the definition of the United Nations Convention. Torture is defined as any intentional act causing physical or mental pain, inflicted by a State agent or any other person acting in an official capacity. This prohibition aims to prevent the systematic use of torture to punish, intimidate or obtain information. Moreover, it prohibits humiliating or coercive treatment. The African Commission has broadened this interpretation by affirming that Article 5 also protects the minimum conditions of life necessary. The right to legal personality, linked to human dignity, guarantees the right to have rights, essential to the protection of individual rights. Serious violations of life and integrity undermine this dignity and this right. In the context of enforced disappearances, the intentional deprivation of legal protection constitutes a denial of legal personality, preventing legal recognition and the exercise of rights.

In the present case, Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana was the subject of an extrajudicial execution, having been removed from the protection of the law between his abduction on 28 May 2012 and the discovery of his body on 2 June 2012. This removal caused irreparable harm to his life and to his physical and psychological well-being. Consequently, he was deprived of the essence of his person, which constitutes a violation of his dignity and his legal personality.

Article 5 explicitly prohibits torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. Although these concepts are not explicitly defined by the African Charter, they are covered by a United Nations convention. The African Commission has adopted in its jurisprudence the definition provided by Article 1 of the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. Torture is defined as any intentional act causing severe physical or mental pain or suffering in order to obtain information, a confession, punishment, intimidation, coercion or for discriminatory reasons, when inflicted by a public official or a person acting in an official capacity.

In essence, torture is the intentional and systematic infliction of physical or psychological pain and suffering by State agents for the purposes of punishment, intimidation or extraction of information.

Article 5 prohibits not only torture but also cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, which encompasses acts causing severe physical or psychological suffering and those forcing a person to act against his will or conscience.

The African Commission recognises that uncertainty as to the condition and future of a family member can cause acute suffering, which constitutes a violation of Article 5 with respect to the family members. Holding persons without allowing them to contact their family and concealing information about their detention constitutes a violation of Article 5.

Drawing on the jurisprudence relating to enforced disappearances, the uncertainty surrounding the disappearance of a person and the lack of information on his fate cause profound and continuing suffering for relatives.

The Human Rights Committee recognises that the anguish caused by the disappearance constitutes a violation of Article 7 of the Covenant with respect to relatives. A passive response by the State to establishing the circumstances of the disappearance may exacerbate this distress.

In this case, the victim's family has experienced immense suffering, not knowing what the circumstances of his violent death were. The absence of an effective investigation perpetuates this anguish. By this fact, the African Commission recognises this suffering as a violation of Article 5 of the African Charter with respect to the family.

Article 6 of the African Charter stipulates that "[e]very individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained."

In analysing the jurisprudence of the African Commission, it is evident that Article 6 encompasses two distinct but complementary aspects: the right to liberty and the right to security of the person.

The right to liberty extends to every individual and constitutes a fundamental condition for enjoying other rights. The African Commission explains that deprivation of liberty has direct and undesirable repercussions on the enjoyment of several other rights, such as the right to a family, to privacy, to freedom of assembly, association, expression, and even the right to freedom of movement.

It implies the right to be free from any constraint, subject to compliance with the law. Thus, Article 6 of the African Charter protects individuals against arbitrary arrest and detention. The African Commission stresses that this article must be interpreted so as to authorise arrests only in the exercise of the powers normally vested in law enforcement forces in a democratic society.

The African Commission provides criteria for determining the arbitrary nature of a detention. Arbitrariness must not simply be unlawful, but must also be interpreted more broadly to include inappropriateness, injustice, lack of predictability and of established procedure.

Examples of violations of liberty include arrest and incommunicado detention, detention without charge and being brought before a court, detention incompatible with international human rights standards, as well as arrests on ethnic grounds.

The right to security, also protected by Article 6 of the African Charter, is considered an expression of rights based on the prohibition of torture and cruel and unusual punishment. It refers to the obligation of the State to protect the physical integrity of its citizens against abuses by public authorities.

Several positive obligations flow from the right to liberty and security. The State must protect individuals against violations of their liberty and security, prevent such violations, investigate when they occur, prosecute and punish the perpetrators, and grant full reparation to the victims.

In the case of Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana, several violations of his liberty and security were found. Death threats were made against him because of his political affiliation, and his abduction constituted an arbitrary deprivation of liberty. The State, by not taking the appropriate measures to protect the victim, failed in its obligation of protection.
Consequently, the African Commission finds a violation of Article 6 of the African Charter with respect to Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana.

Under Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter, "[e]very individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force".

The African Commission has interpreted this article as recognising for complainants the right to have "unhindered access to a competent court or tribunal to hear their case". According to the jurisprudence developed, a competent body is a body holding the power - by law - to investigate the case and to try the person subject to prosecution. The rights protected in Article 7(1)(a) are recognised for persons arrested and detained, but also for any other individual.

The African Commission has considered that when victims are prevented from accessing the courts to have their case heard, State authorities violate Article 7(1) of the African Charter. It has thus affirmed that when the competent authorities place obstacles to the access of victims to the courts, they must be held responsible.

The analysis of the jurisprudence provides examples of obstacles that could prevent victims' access to the courts. This includes the expulsion of refugees without giving them the opportunity to be heard by the national judicial bodies, as well as situations where houses are burned down, bombings and acts of violence are committed against the victims, thus making access to the competent bodies illusory and impossible. In these cases, the Commission considered that the authorities violated Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter.

Furthermore, Article 26 of the African Charter imposes on States the duty to guarantee the independence of the courts, an essential component to guarantee victims an effective remedy before domestic judicial institutions. The Commission has already found a violation of Articles 7(1) and 26 of the African Charter in situations where the impartiality of the courts is not guaranteed.

In the present case, despite the mobilisation of NGOs and the request for a thorough, independent investigation and for the prosecution of the perpetrators, no effective and complete investigation was conducted. The local remedies pursued proved ineffective and unsatisfactory, demonstrating that the cause was not heard.
Consequently, the African Commission finds a violation of Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter with respect to Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana.
Under Article 9(2) of the African Charter, "[e]very individual shall have the right to express and disseminate his opinions within the law."

Freedom of expression, which naturally includes freedom of opinion, has been defined by the Commission as a fundamental human right, crucial for the personal development and political consciousness of an individual, as well as for his effective participation in the public affairs of his country. It is therefore considered an essential pillar of any democratic society. The Commission stresses that in a democratic State, governed by the rule of law, the legitimate exercise of human rights should pose no problem.

The jurisprudence of the African Commission confirms that Article 9 of the African Charter protects the expression of political opinions. No exception to this freedom is provided for by the Charter, even in the event of a serious and imminent threat to national security.

The Commission has adopted a jurisprudence that vigorously defends freedom of opinion and expression. It affirms that any restriction on these rights must be minimal and must not compromise the fundamental rights guaranteed by international law.

The Commission has already concluded that the execution of political opponents constitutes a total restriction on freedom of expression, thus violating Article 9 of the African Charter. It also considers that ill-treating individuals for having expressed political opinions contrary to the State constitutes a violation of freedom of expression. Likewise, persecuting individuals because of their affiliation with opposition political parties amounts to a violation of Article 9.

In the present case, the execution of Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana because of his political opinions and his active involvement in the MSD constitutes, according to the jurisprudence of the African Commission, a total restriction on freedom of expression, thus resulting in a violation of Article 9(2) of the Charter.
Under Article 10(1) of the African Charter, "[e]very individual shall have the right to free association provided that he abides by the law."

In its Resolution on the Right to Freedom of Association, the African Commission specified that when regulating the exercise of the right to freedom of association, the competent authorities should not impose measures that may restrict this freedom. Moreover, it stressed that the regulation of this exercise should respect the obligations of States under the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights.

Freedom of association mainly implies that the State refrains from any interference in the free formation of associations. Consequently, the Commission held that the general prohibition of any assembly for political purposes in all places, as well as the very prohibition of the formation of political parties, constitute a violation of Article 10(1). Likewise, imprisoning or persecuting individuals simply for their affiliation with an opposition movement is considered a violation of freedom of association.

Consequently, in accordance with the jurisprudence of the Commission, it is necessary to consider that in this particular situation, the persecution and execution of Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana because of his affiliation with an opposition party constitute a violation of freedom of association protected by Article 10(1).

Article 18(1) of the African Charter stipulates that the family is the natural unit and basis of society, and that it must be protected by the State, which must take care of its physical health and moral.

The African Commission has already established that the separation of family members due to arbitrary and secret detention constitutes a violation of the right to family life, and therefore of Article 18(1) of the African Charter.

In the present case, the execution of Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana entailed a break-up of the family unit and violated the psychological health of the members of his family, in particular his sister and his widowed father. They suffered deeply from his loss, all the more so as the circumstances surrounding his death are particularly violent and remain unclarified to date. The fact that those responsible have not been clearly identified or prosecuted further aggravates their pain.

In her testimony, published in an article in 2013 and submitted by the Complainants, the sister of Mr. Juvénal, in despair at the void left by his absence, expresses the deep pain felt and the impossibility of filling the void caused by the loss of her brother. As for their father, already a widower, he will never recover from this loss. The sister explains further that other witnesses exist, but that their testimony has become increasingly difficult to obtain because of fear for their safety, given the support enjoyed by the accused.
Consequently, the African Commission finds a violation of Article 18(1) of the African Charter with respect to the relatives of Mr. Juvénal Havyarimana. The Commission,
For these reasons, declares that the State of Burundi has violated the provisions of Articles 2; 4; 5; 6; 7(1) and 26 read together; 9(2); 10(1) and 18(1). Consequently, the Commission

Urges the Republic of Burundi to initiate a thorough and effective investigation into the execution of the victim and the other violations suffered, with the aim of instituting criminal proceedings against the perpetrators of the acts and bringing them to justice.
Requests the Republic of Burundi to provide adequate reparation to the beneficiaries of the victim. This would include measures such as financial compensation for material and non-material damage.

Requires Burundi to report, within three months, on the measures taken in response to the conclusions of the African Commission Adopted at the 78th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights held from 23 February to 8 March 2024, by virtual means CONFIDENTIAL

Le Secrétariat de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (le Secrétariat) a reçu le 3 octobre 2018, une Communication introduite par l'Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (IHRDA) et l'Association des Femmes avocates défenseures des Droits Humains (les Plaintants), pour le compte de 1016 personnes (les victimes) dont 837 femmes et 179 hommes.

Les personnes ci-dessus citées (ci-après dénommées « victimes »), toutes de nationalités congolaises sont celles contre lesquelles les violations ont été commises et pour le compte desquelles la présente plainte a été introduite.

La Plainte a été introduite contre l'Etat de la République Démocratique du Congo (RDC) (ci-après dénommée Etat défendeur ou la RDC), Etat ayant ratifié la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Charte africaine) le 20 juillet 1987 et le Protocole à la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples relatifs aux droits de la femme en Afrique (Protocole de Maputo) le 9 juin 2008.

Les Plaintants indiquent que ces violations des droits de l'homme à l'endroit des victimes ont été perpétrées par les militaires des Forces Armées Congolaises (FARDC) entre le 20 novembre 2012 et le 2 janvier 2013 en pleine période d'un conflit armé les opposant aux rebelles du M23 dans la Province du Nord-Kivu. Ces violations concernent particulièrement des actes d'exactions résultant de pillages généralisés et systématiques, de torture, de coups et blessures volontaires graves, de destruction et d'extorsion des biens, de vol à mains armées, de menaces de mort, de mauvais traitements et d'abus particulièrement violents à l'égard de personnes qui tentaient de s'opposer à la violation de leurs biens et au viol de leurs femmes ou filles.

Les Plaintants rapportent qu'à la suite de ces événements, plusieurs victimes ont bravé la peur de représailles et ont porté plainte devant l'Auditorat Militaire du Sud-Kivu pour que les auteurs qui sont bien identifiés et connus répondent de leurs actes et soient punis conformément à la loi congolaise.

Les Plaintants rapportent, qu'en novembre 2012, les militaires congolais en plein conflit armé décidèrent de s'enfuir face à l'avancée des combattants du M23 qui avaient pris la ville de Goma, située dans la partie Nord-Est de la RDC. Ils ont pris la route de Minova, un grand village situé sur les berges volcaniques du Kivu à la frontière entre les Provinces du Nord et du Sud-Kivu, où ils se sont redéployés.

Il ressort de l'exposé des Plaintants, que sur la route qui les conduisait à Minova-centre en passant par les campements des déplacés de guerre et les villages voisins de Ndosho, Sake, Shasha, Mubambi, Bweremana, Bwisha, Bunagana, Mubimbi, Kashinji, Katoko, Ruchunda, Kalungu, Mushaki, Kirwa, Bungulube, Buragiza, les soldats des FARDC, furieux, humiliés et démoralisés se sont lancés dans une folie destructrice durant plus de 10 jours avec comme conséquences néfastes : des viols, des actes de tortures, des homicides intentionnels, des attaques contre les personnes civiles, des violences sexuelles, des pillages systématiques de maisons, des kiosques et bétail, des extorsions des biens, des destructions de biens, vols à mains armées et à grande échelle, occupation illégale des terres appartenant aux communautés rurales, la dégradation des champs et d'habitats appartenant soit aux résidents, soit aux personnes déplacées de guerre installées dans les camps de fortune, soit aux personnes civiles fuyant la guerre.

Selon les déclarations des victimes, les auteurs de ces violations massives des droits de l'homme étaient environ 6.000 à 8.000 militaires appartenant aux unités des FARDC qui combattaient les rebelles de M23 au mois de novembre 2012 au Nord-Kivu et qui s'étaient enfuis vers MINOVA et environs vers mi-novembre 2012. Ces unités sont les suivantes : - Les 804 et 810 Régiments, les 391 et 41 Régiments Commandos et Bataillons de la 8 Région Militaire du Nord-Kivu ; le 10062 Bataillon de la 10 Région Militaire du Sud-Kivu envoyé en renfort ; les Militaires du 802 Régiment et les militaires du 82 Secteur ; et la Garde Républicaine. Ce premier groupe a été déployé afin de défendre l'aéroport de Goma. Ceux-ci ont tenu leurs positions sur place à Goma jusqu'au 19 novembre 2012 puis ils se sont enfuis vers Minova. - Le 393 Bataillon Commando, sous le commandement opérationnel de la 8 Région militaire. Ce groupe a été envoyé en mission opérationnelle sur place à Minova afin d'établir un contrôle dans l'hypothèse où le M23 aurait lancé une attaque depuis le territoire de Masisi.

Les plaignants ajoutent que quelques mois après le retrait partiel des troupes des FARDC sur Minova, l'Etat congolais y a envoyé successivement l'Auditorat Supérieur du Nord-Kivu et celui du Sud-Kivu pour amorcer les enquêtes conjointes sur toutes ces violations des droits humains perpétrées dans Minova et villages environnants. Commencées vers fin novembre 2012, les enquêtes judiciaires pré-juridictionnelles se sont clôturées au niveau des Auditorats militaires opérationnels en avril 2013. Elles ont connu beaucoup d'interruptions au motif que les militaires poursuivis étaient tous allés sur d'autres fronts pour combattre le M23 et qu'il fallait les entendre pour ouvrir les dossiers à leur charge.

Les Plaignants rapportent que les Auditorats Militaires du Sud et Nord Kivu ont constitué un dossier unique après instruction pré-juridictionnelle sous le N° RMP 0372/BBM/013 qui fut transmis aux prévenus sélectionnés au bout d'une enquête partielle ayant écarté les vrais auteurs des crimes, des milliers de victimes éloignées ainsi qu'une dizaine de villages martyrs et camps des déplacés démantelés qui ont subi des préjudices comme MINOVA. Ils réitérèrent que ce dossier contenait des décisions de renvoi contradictoires et des procès-verbaux incomplets et inintelligibles rédigés par les Auditeurs militaires peu expérimentés en matière d'enquêtes sur les violations des droits de l'homme, qui ne comprenaient pas les patois des victimes et qui craignaient pour leur propre sécurité.

Le dossier aux fins de fixation fut transmis en date du 5 novembre 2013, soit après 12 mois d'attente, au greffe près de la Cour Militaire Opérationnelle du Nord-Kivu territorialement compétente et qui a enrôlé le dossier sous le N° RP003/2013 MP et PC (1016) c/Nzale Nkumu Ngandu et 38 autres/Minova-Bweremana.

Ils rapportent que tous les officiers poursuivis, à l'exception d'un seul, ont été accusés de viol, de pillage et d'homicide en tant que crimes de guerre commis par des troupes placées sous leurs ordres. Plusieurs autres accusations étaient portées à l'encontre des 25 soldats de rang (militaires qui ne sont pas des officiers), notamment celles de crimes de guerre par viol et pillage. Au cours du procès, toutes les parties furent valablement représentées : l'Etat congolais civilement responsable était représenté par ses avocats et les victimes étaient représentées et/ou assistées par le collectif de leurs conseils pris en charge par les ONGs Association du Barreau Américain et Avocats Sans Frontières. Les prévenus quant à eux étaient représentés par leurs avocats pris en charge par le Programme des Nations Unies pour le Développement (PNUD). La Cour Militaire Opérationnelle a mené l'instruction durant 5 mois, à partir du 20 novembre 2013.

Les Plaintants rapportent que c'est après une longue attente du verdict que la Cour Militaire Opérationnelle (CMO) prononça l'Arrêt RP 003/2013, au bout de 2 ans et 5 mois de procédure allant de décembre 2012 à mai 2014. L'arrêt a été prononcé le 5 mai 2014 à Goma, en présence de quelques prévenus seulement et en l'absence des victimes ou de leurs avocats. Sur les 39 accusés, seuls deux soldats de rang inférieur ont été reconnus coupables d'avoir commis un viol en tant que crime de droit commun. Les 14 officiers de grade supérieur, le chef d'Etat-major de la Force Terrestre ou encore les Commandants de compagnies qui assumaient la responsabilité en tant que supérieurs hiérarchiques des troupes depuis Goma jusqu'à Minova et ses environs dans leur ensemble, ont été mis hors de cause alors que lors de leurs auditions, certains d'entre eux étaient passés aux aveux. Les 9 autres officiers de grade inférieur qui avaient aussi été inculpés pour des faits graves des violences sexuelles systématiques ont tous été acquittés. Au total, il y a eu 23 acquittements et seulement 16 condamnations de certains soldats de rang qui ont été reconnus coupables de pillage en tant que crime de guerre.

Cet arrêt de la CMO n'a jamais été signifié aux parties civiles qui s'étaient régulièrement constituées. Il y a également lieu de noter que cet arrêt n'est pas susceptible d'appel ni d'opposition conformément à l'article 87 de la loi n° 023/2002 du 18 novembre 2002 portant code judiciaire militaire qui dispose que : « les arrêts rendus par les Cours Militaires Opérationnelles ne sont susceptibles d'aucun recours », disposition complétée par l'Ordonnance présidentielle qui a implanté et autorisé d'office cette Cour Opérationnelle dans les zones opérationnelles du Nord-Kivu. En d'autres termes, les victimes très mécontentes de l'Arrêt RP 003/2013 ne peuvent faire ni appel ni opposition car cet arrêt a été rendu en premier et dernier ressort.

Les Plaintants affirment que cette plainte n'a pas été soumise à un autre organe international de règlement de litiges ou doté d'une compétence similaire conformément à l'article 56(7) de la Charte Africaine.

Les Plaintants allèguent la violation des articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 14, 16 et 16 de la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des Peuples (la Charte africaine) et 3, 4, 8, 11, 14, 24 et 25 du Protocole à la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples relatif aux droits des femmes (le Protocole de Maputo).

Les Plaintants demandent à la Commission de : a. Examiner la présente Communication en vertu des articles 55 et 56 de la Charte africaine. b. Conclure que le gouvernement congolais s'est rendu coupable de violations des articles 1, 5, 6, 7, 14 et 16 de la Charte africaine et 3, 4, 11, 14, 16 et 19 du Protocole de Maputo. c. Tenir l'Etat congolais pour responsable des actes commis par ses préposés et le condamner à la réparation de tous les préjudices par eux causés. d. Enjoindre au gouvernement congolais de poursuivre et punir les auteurs des violations conformément au code pénal congolais.
La Plainte est parvenue au Secrétariat de la Commission africaine le 3 octobre 2018, qui en a accusé réception le même jour.

Lors de sa 63 Session ordinaire tenue du 23 octobre au 13 novembre 2018 à Banjul, en Gambie, la Commission a examiné la Plainte et a décidé de l'admettre. Le 16 novembre 2018, le Secrétariat a informé les parties de cette décision et a demandé aux Plaintants de soumettre leurs moyens sur la recevabilité de la Communication, conformément à l'article 105 (1) du règlement intérieur de la Commission (2010).

Le 22 janvier 2019, le Secrétariat a reçu des Plaintants une requête en extension du délai de soumission de leurs observations sur la recevabilité. Le Secrétariat a informé les Plaintants qu'un délai d'un mois leur a été accordé conformément aux dispositions de l'article 113(2) du Règlement intérieur de la Commission (2010).

Le 22 février 2019, les Plaintants ont transmis au Secrétariat leurs observations sur la recevabilité. A la même date, le Secrétariat a transmis lesdites observations à l'Etat défendeur et requis sa réponse dans un délai de soixante (60) jours. L'Etat défendeur n'ayant pas respecté ce délai, le Secrétariat lui a notifié qu'il disposait d'un ultime délai de trente (30) jours pour soumettre, faute de quoi la Commission rendrait une décision par défaut.

Lors de ses sessions successives tenues entre avril 2019 et avril 2022, la Commission a examiné la Communication et décidé de renvoyer sa décision sur la Recevabilité pour défaut de soumission par l'Etat défendeur. Les correspondances requises ont été adressées aux Parties.

Lors de sa 71 Session ordinaire tenue virtuellement du 21 avril au 13 mai 2022, la Commission a examiné la Communication et l'a déclarée recevable par défaut. Les Parties en ont été informées et les observations des Plaintants sur le fond requises dans les délais prévus par le Règlement intérieur.

Lors de sa 72 Session ordinaire tenue virtuellement du 19 juillet au 2 août 2022, la Commission a examiné la Communication et a décidé de renvoyer sa décision sur le fond pour attendre les observations des parties. Cette décision a été communiquée aux parties le 13 août 2022 et les observations des Plaintants ont été requises.
