They also say that the victims are stigmatized by the community, which calls them "Wakubakwa" to designate a raped person. The same is true of the children who are ostracized at school.

The Complainants maintain that by ratifying the African Charter, the DRC undertook to take all measures to prevent the violation of the rights it sets out and, where appropriate, to remedy their disregard by its agents or by any other person under its authority. They reiterate that by violating its obligations arising from the various provisions of the Charter and the Maputo Protocol, the State violated Article 1 of the Charter
The Respondent State has not submitted its observations on the merits despite multiple reminders from the Secretariat of the Commission inviting it to do so.

As indicated above, the Respondent State has not submitted its observations on the Complainants' allegations. In the absence of these observations, the Commission will pursue its analysis on the basis of the elements at its disposal; this in accordance with its already established jurisprudence.

Before any analysis on the merits of the Complainants' allegations, it is important for the Commission to establish the scope of its competence under the Charter. Indeed, in the present Communication, in addition to the allegations of violation of the African Charter, the Complainants invite the Commission to find the violation of the provisions of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa, known as the Maputo Protocol. It is therefore incumbent on the Commission to verify its competence to interpret this Protocol.

Article 27 of the Maputo Protocol on its interpretation indicates that "the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights shall be seized with matters of interpretation arising from the application or implementation of this Protocol". This provision implies that in the event of a conflict of interpretation of the Maputo Protocol, it is the Court that is competent to decide. However, this does not mean that the Commission is not competent to interpret this instrument for the protection of women's rights in Africa.

Indeed, by its expression "Protocol to the Charter", the Maputo Protocol is a supplement to and consequently forms an integral part of the African Charter. This follows even from Article 66 of the Charter which provides for the adoption of special protocols or agreements, if necessary, to "supplement the provisions of the present Charter". In particular, the Maputo Protocol finds its raison d'être or legal basis in the provisions of Article 18(3) of the Charter which requires all States to eliminate all forms of discrimination against women and to ensure the protection of women's rights, as stipulated in international declarations and conventions. It therefore supplements the Charter in its Article 18(3).

The status of the Maputo Protocol as a supplement to the Charter is also deduced from its Article 26 which requires States to incorporate in their periodic reports submitted in accordance with the terms of Article 62 of the African Charter, indications of the legislative and other measures they have taken for the full realization of the rights recognized in the Maputo Protocol.

Thus, the Commission being vested with the power to interpret the principal instrument that is the Charter, it follows that it is also so vested for the document that supplements it, namely, therefore, the Maputo Protocol.

The Commission observes that in reality, all the Complainants' allegations are linked to the ineffectiveness of the appeal made by the convicted persons before the High Military Court. Indeed, the Commission notes that whereas the 1 Judge had admitted the violations alleged by the Complainants and had convicted the accused, the procedure before the High Military Court (appellate court) has been indefinitely long. In particular, although there were several hearings in 2015, the Commission notes from the Complainants' submissions that many others were postponed and no decision on the merits has been rendered. Also the victims are and remain drowned in dilatory procedural manoeuvres preventing them from having the first judge's convictions enforced. It is for this reason that it proposes to analyze first the allegation of violation of the right of access to justice and the right to a fair trial

The Complainants allege the violation of Article 7(1) of the African Charter and of Article 8(a) and (e) of the Maputo Protocol. 106.Article 7(1) provides: "1. Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts of violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force; (b) The right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty by a competent court or tribunal; (c) The right to defence, including the right to be defended by counsel of his choice; (d) The right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal." 107.In the case of Kevin Mgwanga Gunme et al v. Cameroon, the Commission indicated that respect for the rights set out in Article 7 is a fundamental principle in any democratic State. The Commission considers that it is through respect for these rights that the other rights guaranteed by the Charter can be realized. Thus, it is important that States take rigorous measures to ensure their application or to enable their respect. 108.The right to be tried within a reasonable time includes the expression "reasonable time" which needs to be clarified in order to understand its scope and content. Unfortunately, the Charter does not give its meaning. However, the Commission first notes that this expression contains a juxtaposition of two terms: that of "time" and that of "reasonable". In essence, the term "time" means an interval of time during which an action occurs. Thus, it can be deduced that, in the context of judicial proceedings, "time" means an interval of time in which a trial, a judgment or a judicial decision takes place. 109.As for the qualifier "reasonable", it refers to what is logical and satisfactory. It follows that the term "reasonable time" as intended by the Charter refers to an interval of time that is neither surprisingly long nor abusively short. In other words, the Charter wants the duration of the trial to be of an acceptable length or not excessively long or else the trial to be concluded without excessive delay.

However, it remains important to determine what represents a delay that is not excessive. In its Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa adopted in 2003, the Commission indicated that to determine the possible existence of excessive delay, account must be taken notably of the complexity of the case, the conduct of the parties, the conduct of other participants in the proceedings, the conduct of the competent authorities, whether or not a person is in pre-trial detention and the interest of the person concerned in the proceedings. The Commission therefore considers that the circumstances of the case, notably the complexity of the case, the conduct of the authorities and of the trial in general, are an important element in determining whether the length of a trial is reasonable.

In the case under analysis, the Commission observes that the Military Court of South Kivu had convicted the perpetrators on 21 February 2011. The latter lodged an appeal on the spot the same day, that is to say the 2011 before the High Military Court. However, the Commission also notes that at the time of receipt of the Complainants' observations on the merits on 26 July 2022, that is about 10 years after it was seized, the High Military Court had not yet rendered its decision although hearings had taken place in 2015.

The Commission notes that there were no particular circumstances that contributed to such a delay as defined above. In this sense, it considers that this waiting period is not reasonable. This violation of the right to a remedy thus led to the actualization of all the other violations alleged and admitted by the first judge. The State therefore took back with one hand what it had granted with the other.
Hence the violation of Article 7(1) of the Charter On the violation of Article 8(a) and (e) of the Maputo Protocol

Article 8(a) and (e) of the Maputo Protocol provides that "women and men are equal before the law and shall have the right to equal protection and benefit of the law. States shall take all appropriate measures to ensure: a) effective access by women to legal and judicial assistance and services; e) equitable representation of women in the judicial institutions and those responsible for law enforcement". This provision advocates the right of access to justice and the right to equal protection of women before the law.

The Commission considers that this right preaches the non-discrimination of women before the law. In particular, the right of access to justice and to equal protection of women before the law consists in the right of women or any other person to have access to the courts and to be treated or protected in the same way by the law and the courts. Thus, this provision prevents protection by the courts or the law from being denied to women on the pretext that they are women while men benefit from it. The Commission considers that, for there to be a violation of Article 8(a) and (e), it must be demonstrated that women did not benefit from the same protection as men from the courts or the law.

In this case, the Commission does not find in the Complainants' submissions elements that show that women were victims of treatment different from that of men before the courts or the law. In particular, it is not demonstrated that the excessive delay or unreasonable time taken by the High Military Court to decide on the situation of the victims was due to their social status as women. More specifically, that legal assistance or legal or judicial services were denied to the women victims of these attacks for the sole reason of belonging to the category of "women".

In the absence of this proof, the Commission concludes that Article 8(a) and (e) was not violated. On the alleged violation of the right not to be subjected to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment and the right to dignity

The Complainants allege the violation of Article 5 of the African Charter and of Article 3(1) of the Maputo Protocol. Article 5 of the Charter guarantees respect for human dignity and prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment in these terms: "Every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited". As for Article 3(1) of the Maputo Protocol, it provides that "Every woman shall have the right to dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition and protection of her human and legal rights."

The Complainants allege that the blows and injuries inflicted on the 52 victims of Fizi constitute torture within the meaning of the Convention against Torture. It is important for the Commission to understand the content and meaning of Article 5 of the Charter and of Article 3(1) of the Maputo Protocol.

The Commission observes that the two provisions are interconnected and complement each other in that they both contribute to respect for human dignity. Indeed, whereas Article 5 advocates respect for the dignity of every individual, Article 3(1) of the Protocol is specific because it advocates the dignity of women. Article 5 of the Charter lists certain attitudes that lead to the violation of human dignity including, among others, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment which are alleged by the Complainants in the present communication. The Commission is of the view that dignity is a concept around which the prohibition of torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment is founded. Indeed, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment necessarily violates human dignity.

Neither the Charter nor the Maputo Protocol defines the notion of torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment. In the absence of such a definition by the Charter, the Commission can only draw inspiration from other international human rights instruments under Articles 60 and 61 of the Charter. Thus, Article 1 of the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment indicates that the term "torture" "means any act by which severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted on a person for such purposes as obtaining from him or a third person information or a confession, punishing him for an act he or a third person has committed or is suspected of having committed, or intimidating or coercing him or a third person, or for any reason based on discrimination of any kind, when such pain or suffering is inflicted by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity. It does not include pain or suffering arising only from, inherent in or incidental to lawful sanctions".

Thus, the Commission notes that this definition contains three cumulative conditions in order to be able to conclude that torture exists. First, torture involves the intentional infliction of severe suffering which may be physical or mental. This is what the United Nations Human Rights Committee emphasized in its general comment No. 20 in interpreting Article 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights which prohibits torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment. In that general comment, the Committee indicated that this article "relates not only to acts that cause physical pain but also to acts that cause mental suffering" Next, this infliction must be administered by a public official or any person acting in an official capacity or at his instigation or with his express or tacit consent, and finally the infliction must be done for a specific purpose.

As for the notion of "cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment", the Commission, in the case of Media Rights v. Nigeria, stressed that "the expression 'cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment' is to be interpreted so as to extend to the widest possible protection against abuses, whether physical or mental".

In this case, from the Complainants' submissions and the testimonies at its disposal, the Commission notes that physical and mental violence was indeed inflicted on the victims. These notably include "gang rapes imposed on women in the presence of their husbands and children, extortions, malicious destruction, damage to or deterioration of property, blows with rifle butts or daggers on targeted persons.....". 125.The Commission shares the Complainants' view that these acts were intentional, because it is manifest that the perpetrators (that is, the soldiers) administered them to the victims as punishment for their alleged role in the death of Pedro. It follows that all these inflictions were made only for the purpose of punishing the victims following the death of Corporal Pedro. The Commission also notes that these acts were inflicted by a public authority, namely the Congolese law enforcement forces, in particular the soldiers. Moreover, in its general comment No. 4, the Commission expressly referred to acts of sexual and gender-based violence as a form of torture and ill-treatment because of the specific, traumatic and gender-specific impact of sexual violence on the victims, including at the individual, family and collective levels. 126.It follows that all the conditions are met to conclude that there was torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment and, consequently, an infringement of the human dignity of the victims who are the women in the present case. 127.The Commission concludes that Articles 5 of the Charter and 3(1) of the Maputo Protocol were violated 128.Under this allegation, the Complainants invoke the violation of Article 6 of the African Charter and of Article 4(1) of the Maputo Protocol

The Complainant alleges the violation of Article 6 of the Charter which stipulates that: "Every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained". The provisions of this article protect both the right to liberty of the person and the right to security of the person. Both rights are fundamental.

Indeed, the enjoyment of these two rights plays an important role in that it influences the enjoyment of other rights. This was, moreover, emphasized by the United Nations Human Rights Committee in its general comment No. 35, indicating that liberty and security of person are precious in themselves and also because the deprivation of liberty and the denial of the right to security of person have at all times been means of impeding the enjoyment of other rights.

In the case of Amnesty International and Others v. Sudan, the Commission indicated that Article 6 must be interpreted so as to permit arrests only in the exercise of the powers normally devolved on law enforcement in a democratic society. Likewise, in the case of Liesbeth Zegveld and Mussie Ephrem v. Eritrea, the African Commission stressed that all detentions must respect fundamental human rights principles. There should be no incommunicado detention and States must indicate that someone is detained by specifying the place of detention. In the Communication Purohit and Moore v. The Gambia also, the African Commission pointed out that the deprivation of liberty must be authorized by law and must be compatible with the obligations of States Parties to the African Charter.

It follows from these assertions of the Commission that the right to liberty and security of person within the meaning of Article 6 means that arrests and detentions must be carried out in strict compliance with the law. However, compliance with the law is not sufficient in itself, it is also necessary that these laws be acceptable in a democratic society.

In this case, after analysis of all the documents and the various testimonies, the Commission first observes that almost all the victims were subjected to unlawful arrest and detention in their homes and in the bush by the soldiers deployed to avenge the death of Corporal Pedro. During these arrests, these victims were raped, some of them in front of their husbands and their children. Others were beaten to force them to accept sexual relations.

From the foregoing, the Commission concludes that the arrests to which the victims were subjected did not comply with the law, since not only were they carried out in their homes and in the bush, but they were also accompanied by acts of rape and human rights violations.
It follows that Article 6 of the Charter was violated. On the alleged violation of Article 4(1) of the Maputo Protocol

The Complainants allege the violation of Article 4(1) of the Maputo Protocol which stipulates that "every woman shall be entitled to respect for her life, her physical integrity and the security of her person. All forms of exploitation, punishment and inhuman or degrading treatment shall be prohibited". This provision protects the right to life, to physical integrity and to the security of women.

The United Nations Human Rights Committee has emphasized that "the right to life concerns the entitlement of individuals to be free from acts and omissions that are intended or may be expected to cause their unnatural or premature death, as well as to enjoy a life with dignity". As for physical integrity, the Commission considers that it is infringed when acts of torture, inhuman or degrading treatment or any kind of barbarity are inflicted on a human being. This implies that respect for physical integrity ensures the protection of the human body and of human life. The right to human security, for its part, protects the human person against any serious and widespread threat.

Thus, through its Article 4(1), the Maputo Protocol wants the life, physical integrity and security of women to be respected in all respects. As the Commission has already indicated in the case of Geneviève Mbiankeu v. Cameroon, States are bound not only by the obligation to respect the rights of their citizens but also to protect them against violation by third parties. Thus, in the case of World Organisation Against Torture and African Zone League for the Defence of the Rights of Children and Students (on behalf of Céline) v. Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Commission considered that the acts of physical violence and gang rape perpetrated against the victim undoubtedly constitute a violation of her physical and moral integrity.

In the present communication, as demonstrated above, the victims faced acts of torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment resulting from the gang rapes inflicted on them. This constitutes an infringement of physical integrity.
It follows that Article 4(1) of the Maputo Protocol was violated
The Complainants allege the violation of Article 14 of the Charter and of Articles 16 and 19(c) of the Maputo Protocol.

This article provides that "The right to property shall be guaranteed. It may only be encroached upon in the interest of public need or in the general interest of the community and in accordance with the provisions of appropriate laws". On analysis of the provisions of this article, the Commission observes that the latter establishes two aspects of the right to property: that is, the principle of the right to property and peaceful enjoyment of goods on the one hand; and the possibility and conditions of this right to property on the other hand.

The African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights defined the right to property by indicating that, in its classical acceptation, this right comprises three elements, namely the right to use the thing which is the object of the right (usus), the right to enjoy its fruits (fructus), and the right to dispose of it, that is to transfer it (abusus). It is in this sense that the Commission considers that the right to property includes not only the right to have access to one's property and to prevent the invasion and encroachment of the said property, but also the right to possession, and use as well as control in complete tranquillity of this property, as its owners desire.

However, Article 14 of the Charter recognizes that States are permitted, in certain circumstances, to control notably the use of property in accordance with the public or general interest, by applying the laws they consider necessary for this purpose.

Thus, in the case of George Iyanyori Kajikabi v. Arab Republic of Egypt, the Commission observed that the chaotic circumstances in which the victims were displaced did not allow them to take their personal effects and that they were forced to abandon them behind them. It also noted that, since the valuables were not returned to them and adequate compensation in respect of the destruction of their personal effects was not granted to them, the State violated Article 14 of the Charter.

In the present communication, the Commission observes that the looting and the attacks carried out by the FARDC caused the destruction of houses, shops and numerous other goods including thefts, extortion of telephones and shops, malicious destruction, deterioration of property. The Commission is of the view that all these acts are such as to impede the right to use the thing that is the object of property and do not allow the owners to enjoy its fruits peacefully. The same is true of the right to dispose of or transfer goods over which the victims had the right of property. Indeed, the appropriation of the victims' goods by the perpetrators in the present case contradicts the right to dispose of the thing over which one has the right of property because it is done without the consent of the victims. Thus, the Commission concludes that the right to property as described above was violated in all its aspects.
It follows that Article 14 of the Charter was violated

Article 16 of the Maputo Protocol stipulates as follows: "Women shall have the right to equal access to housing and to acceptable living conditions in a healthy environment. To ensure this right, States Parties shall grant to women, whatever their marital status, access to adequate housing". This article protects the right to housing for women on an equal footing with men.

In its Principles and Guidelines on the Implementation of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in the African Charter, the Commission defined the human right to adequate housing as "the right of everyone to gain and sustain a safe and secure home and community in which to live in peace and dignity". In the SERAC case, the Commission indicated that at a bare minimum, the right to housing obliged the Nigerian government not to destroy the houses of its citizens.

It thus considered that the obligation to respect housing rights requires that the State, and therefore all its organs and agents, abstain from carrying out, sponsoring or tolerating practices, policies or legal measures violating the integrity of individuals or encroaching on their freedom to use this material or other resources available to them, in the manner they find most appropriate to satisfy the housing needs of the individual, family, household or community. Within the meaning of Article 16 of the Maputo Protocol, women must be protected against such practices, policies and legal measures that block the use of their homes in any way.

As explained in the SERAC case, the right to shelter goes even further than a roof over one's head and encompasses the right of every individual to be left alone and to live in peace whether under a roof or not. In the present case, it emerges from the testimonies and the Complainants' submissions that some of the victims' houses were burned, others demolished. As indicated above, all these acts violate the right to housing. Indeed, from all these acts, it is understood that the victims could not live in peace regardless of whether they were under a roof or not.
It follows that Article 16 of the Maputo Protocol was violated On the violation of Article 19(c) of the Maputo Protocol

Article 19(c) of the Maputo Protocol obliges all States Parties to take all appropriate measures to promote women's access to and control over productive resources such as land and to guarantee their right to property. This article protects one of the aspects of the right to sustainable development of women in Africa. It aims notably at the promotion of women's economic rights and independence.

In particular, States must put in place legislation and administrative practices so that women enjoy on an equal footing the same rights as men over economic resources, notably equal access to ownership of land and other property, to credit, to inheritance, to natural resources and to new appropriate techniques. In other words, this provision invites States to contribute to facilitating the independent development of women and, consequently, to enabling their economic potential. They must, in particular, make available to them the productive resources necessary for their economic fulfilment.

In the present case, the Commission observes that quite a lot of property belonging to the victims was destroyed. These notably include houses and numerous other effects they contained. The testimonies show notably that thefts, extortions, destruction of shops, theft of money, telephones... characterized the attacks perpetrated by the soldiers. The Commission considers that all these effects constitute productive resources for the victims and concludes that the Respondent State was not in a position to protect them.
It follows that Article 19(c) of the Maputo Protocol was violated
The Complainants allege the violation of Articles 16 of the Charter and of Article 14(1) of the Maputo Protocol.

Article 16 of the Charter provides as follows: "1. Every individual shall have the right to enjoy the best attainable state of physical and mental health. 2. States Parties to the present Charter shall take the necessary measures to protect the health of their people and to ensure that they receive medical attention when they are sick."

In the case of Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and INTERIGHTS v. Egypt, the Commission noted that the right to health functions directly or indirectly as a precondition to all the other human rights recognized by the African Charter. This was also emphasized in the Communication Purohit and Moore v. The Gambia where the Commission indicated that the enjoyment of the right to health as widely understood is vital to all aspects of a person's life and well-being, and is crucial to the realization of all the other fundamental human rights and freedoms. According to the Commission, this right includes the right to health facilities, access to goods and services which must be guaranteed to all, without discrimination of any kind.

The Commission also indicated in its Principles and Guidelines on the Implementation of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights that the right to health also includes the right to be free from unjustified interference, including, among others, the right not to be subjected to torture and other forms of ill-treatment. What is more, in the same principles and guidelines, the Commission indicated that one of the minimum core obligations of the right to health is to prevent violence against women and mitigate its impact on the physical and mental health of survivors.

In this case, as already explained above, the Complainants were subjected to torture and other inhuman and degrading treatment. In this sense, the Commission considers that this constitutes an unjustified interference with the right to health within the meaning of Article 16 of the Charter. In particular, the Commission observes that the gang rapes perpetrated by the FRDC against the victims in the presence of their husbands and children left them with indelible physical and moral after-effects. The Commission notes that, moreover, the Respondent State did nothing to prevent them or to mitigate their impact on their physical or mental health. Yet, as indicated by the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in its general comment No. 14, a State fails in its obligation to protect the right to health when it "fails to take all necessary measures to safeguard persons within their jurisdiction from infringements of the right to health by third parties."
It follows that Article 16 of the African Charter was violated. On the alleged violation of Article 14(1) of the Maputo Protocol

Article 14(1) provides as follows: "States Parties shall ensure that the right to health of women, including sexual and reproductive health is respected and promoted". This provision protects women's rights to sexual and reproductive health. The Maputo Protocol gives details as to the content of these rights by stipulating that these rights include: "a) the right to control their fertility; b) the right to decide whether to have children, the number of children and the spacing of children; c) the right to choose any method of contraception; d) the right to self-protection and to be protected against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV/AIDS; e) the right to be informed on one's health status and on the health status of one's partner, particularly if affected with sexually transmitted infections, including HIV/AIDS, in accordance with internationally recognized standards and best practices; f) the right to family planning education".

The Commission considers that States have an obligation to ensure that all the aspects described above are respected. In particular, States must ensure that laws, policies, administrative procedures and practices, as well as socio-cultural norms and attitudes that impede access to family planning/contraception or the right of women to exercise control over fertility are avoided. The Commission considers that all these elements infringe the woman's right to life, to non-discrimination and to health.

As for the right to self-protection and to be protected against HIV and sexually transmitted infections, it recalls the general obligation of the State to create a favourable legal and social environment enabling women to be in a position to freely and fully realize their right to protect themselves and to be protected. The right to be informed of the health status of one's partner is also crucial. The Commission considers that it "enables women to make informed decisions about their own health, in particular where they could be exposed to serious risks of infection".

In the present case, the Commission observes that although the Complainants assert that some of the victims were infected with HIV/AIDS following the violence they faced, they do not give any supporting documents.
It follows that Article 14.1 of the Maputo Protocol was not violated

The Complainants allege the violation of Article 1 of the Charter which provides that: "The Member States of the Organization of African Unity parties to the present Charter shall recognize the rights, duties and freedoms enshrined in this Charter and shall undertake to adopt legislative or other measures to give effect to them". This provision means purely and simply that States must give effect to the provisions of the Charter. In the present case, the Complainants consider that by ratifying the African Charter, the DRC undertook to ensure respect for the rights protected by this Charter by developing the necessary measures to prevent their violation, and by remedying it in case of violation. They also consider that by violating provisions of the Charter, the DRC also violated Article 1 of the Charter.

As emerges from its well-established jurisprudence, the Commission observes that indeed, the violation of a provision of the Charter implies a violation of Article 1 of the Charter. Thus, a violation of any provision of the Charter automatically constitutes a violation of Article 1 of the Charter insofar as it evidences the failure of the State Party to adopt adequate measures to give effect to the provisions of the African Charter.
Consequently, having already found a violation of the provisions of the Charter, the Commission concludes that Article 1 of the Charter was also violated.

The Complainants request a number of various reparations. The African Charter does not provide a specific provision on reparations in case of found violations of the rights enshrined therein. However, the right to reparations for violation of human rights obligations being a fundamental principle of international law, the Commission considers that it goes without saying that any harm must be repaired even in the absence of a legal provision. This was, moreover, recalled by the Permanent Court of International Justice in the following terms: "it is a principle of international law that the breach of an engagement involves an obligation to make reparation in an adequate form. Reparation therefore is the indispensable complement of a failure to apply a convention and there is no necessity for this to be stated in the convention itself."

In its jurisprudence, the Commission has also concluded that any violation of the rights enshrined in the Charter gives rise to a right to reparation. This is so, for example, in the case of Jean-Marie Atangana Mebara v. Republic of Cameroon, where the Commission indicated that reparation may take various forms depending on the rights violated and the circumstances of the case, ranging from administrative, legislative and judicial actions to monetary compensation.

In the present case, the Complainants make a series of requests for reparation. The Commission proposes to analyze them one by one. a. On the declaration of the violation of certain provisions of the Charter and the Maputo Protocol

The Complainants implore the Commission to declare that the Democratic Republic of the Congo violated Articles 1, 5, 6, 7, 14 and 16 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights and Articles 3(1), 4(1), 8(a) and (e), 14(1), 16, and 19(c) of the Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Women in Africa.

As already developed, the Commission found the violations of the provisions of the Charter indicated above and of certain other provisions of the Maputo Protocol. It follows that the Commission is justified in making a declaration. b. On the recommendation that the Respondent State prosecute the perpetrators and enforce the decision of the High Military Court

The Complainants request the Commission to recommend that the DRC prosecute and punish the perpetrators of the violations within six months from the notification of the decision on the merits, and ensure the immediate enforcement of the judgment of the High Military Court once rendered. They also request that this enforcement be carried out without prejudice to subsequent recommendations issued by the African Commission.

The Commission wishes to recall that one of the obligations of States to ensure the implementation of human rights is the "obligation to protect". Under this obligation, States are required to ensure that the enjoyment by every person, without discrimination, of all human rights is protected against abuses by third parties. Such protection must be achieved not only by the introduction of laws and measures aimed at protecting human rights as emerges from Article 1 of the Charter, but also by the establishment of affordable and accessible remedial procedures in case of abuse of these rights.

As the Commission has already stressed in the Communication, Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights & INTERIGHTS v. Egypt, States must above all "put in place normative systems and institutions to maintain a justice system that offers remedies for violations and imposes sanctions on offenders". Thus, in this respect, States must ensure that the persons responsible for any violation are held accountable through administrative, administrative, disciplinary or judicial sanctions, as appropriate or as needed. In this sense, it follows that the Complainants' request is well founded.

The Commission shares the view of the Complainants who wish it to request the Respondent State to enforce the decision of the High Military Court once rendered, without prejudice to the recommendations issued by the African Commission. Indeed, the Commission the commission not being a criminal court to punish the perpetrators of offences, it is the responsibility of States to criminalize them and to ensure that all the sanctions imposed on them are enforced. Moreover, it is the Commission's practice to recommend that the calculation of damages resulting from human rights violations at the end of a communication be made by national courts. The recommendation to have a decision enforced would be in line with this practice.

The Complainants implore the Commission to order the Congolese State to pay the 52 victims the following individual monetary reparations: - 500 000$ to Abwe Ada - 500 000$ to Aimerance Nyassa Bitokenya - 500 000$ to Albertine Mateso Jeanne - 500 000$ to Andjelani Michèle - 500 000$ to Aziza Bunyemu Gizele - 500 000$ to Bahati Tubongye - 500 000$ to Banyeki Bahati Jolie - 500 000$ to Biebebe Naponga Isengelo - 500 000$ to Binti Fundi Malenga - 500 000$ to Byalamu Aamba Roda - 500 000$ to Byamungu Francine - 500 000$ to Eto Asukulo Taci - 600 000$ to Eric Mataba Ntalindwa - 500 000$ to Faila Asende Jeune - 500 000$ to Faila Feza Ngongo - 500 000$ to Bora Ezechiel Hazina - 500 000$ to Jacquéline Mbukani Aziza - 500 000$ to Kashindi Abedi Marie - 500 000$ to Kashindi Walonge Cirezi - 500 000$ to M'lebinge Huseni - 500 000$ Machozi Lusaba - 500 000$ to Machozi Sema Idi - 500 000$ Malibu Sada Shegeko - 500 000$ to Mande Itongelo - 500 000$ Mwajuuma Asumani Mwati - 500 000$ to Martha Furahisha - 500 000$ to Matisho Mulilwa - 500 000$ to Mauwa Ndale Salima - 500 000$ to Mauwa Véronique Esta - 500 000$ to Mawazo Fatuma Walengamina - 500 000$ to Mawazo Mwangaza Jolie - 500 000$ to Mwajuma Kishindi Sireine - 500 000$ to Mwasimuke Alfani Apendeki - 300 000$ to the beneficiaries of Mwavita Mulasi Jeanne - 300 000$ to the beneficiaries of Nyasa Fariala - 500 000$ to Nyota Salima Tantine - 300 000$ to Nzigire Sylvine Ombeni - 500 000$ to Rebecca Sifa Francine - 500 000$ to Mebii Regina Elisabeth Watekwa - 500 000$ to Riziki Alinoti Julie - 500 000$ to Roda Malanda Mamy - 300 000$ to the beneficiaries of Tiba Julita Lwala - 500 000$ to Tosha Abwe Adolphine - 500 000$ to Tosha Etonyema Clémentine - 500 000$ to Tubongye Nambeleci Nyasa - 500 000$ to Ubaaya Mauwa Severine - 500 000$ to Vumilia Nambasha - 500 000$ to Wanyema Sipola Mitamba - 500 000$ to Roda Malanda Mamy - 500 000$ to Zohena Bingibinwa Jacquelina - 500 000$ to Faila Kasindi - 500 000$ to Bora Ezéchiel HAZINA

The Complainants consider that 52 victims suffered material, physical, emotional and moral harm. They mention above all thefts, demolished or burned houses; moral suffering linked to the death of their relatives, to illnesses subsequent to the rapes and torture, to shattered dreams, to reduced physical abilities, to the inability to obtain medical care, to the absence of reparation, to the impunity of the perpetrators, to changes in lifestyle, to vulnerability, to stigmatization, etc. In their submissions on reparations, they give an individualized description of the suffering of each victim and pray the Commission to compensate them in equity taking into account the particular circumstances of each victim and in justice given the impossibility of calculating precisely all the material and non-material damage that the victims suffered.

The Commission first observes that there is a difficulty in identifying the victims of the acts of human rights violations perpetrated by the soldiers in the locality of FIZI in January 2011. In particular, the Complainants draw up a list of 52 victims. However, the Commission notes that there are victims who are repeated twice as is visible in the list indicated above. This is the case of the victim Bora Ezechiel Hazina (identified as victim 17 and victim 52 in the Complainants' submissions) and the victim Roda Malanda Mamy (identified as victim 41 and victim 49 in the Complainants' submissions).

On analysis of the identification documents in both cases, the Commission finds that the same victims are listed twice and make the same claims. Thus, the Commission being aware of the principle that "reparation must be just, adequate, effective, sufficient, appropriate, victim-oriented and proportionate to the harm suffered", it cannot rule on the calculation of the amount of reparation. Consequently, and as is its practice, it refers this calculation to the national courts, better placed to identify the real victims and the nature of the harm suffered.

The Complainants also request the Commission to order the Congolese State to offer the victims recalled in the point above free and immediate, adequate and effective medical and psychological or psychiatric support, through specialized public health institutions to the victims who request it. They add that in the event that the State does not have the staff or specialized institutions capable of providing the required level of support, it should call upon specialized private institutions. According to them, the treatment must continue as long as the health of the victims requires.

In its General Comment No. 3 on the implementation of Article 14 of the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, the Committee against Torture recalled that the obligation imposed by the Convention to ensure various forms of rehabilitation services does not remove the need to provide medical and psychosocial services to victims directly after acts of torture.

In the present case, it emerges from the various testimonies submitted to the Commission that the victims are confronted with various health problems, notably of a psychological nature. Thus, it is incumbent on the State to put in place a rehabilitation system to ensure for them any medical or psychological treatment they may need.
It follows that the Complainants' request is suitable and acceptable e. On the introduction of a human rights module in the curriculum of a certain category of officials

The Complainants also request the Commission to recommend that the Respondent State include a human rights module in the training curriculum of soldiers, magistrates and other law enforcement officers. Such a module should place particular emphasis on women's rights.

The Commission is in agreement with the Complainants as regards this request and finds that such a module could serve as a remedy for the various abuses committed by the DRC's law enforcement forces, often reported. This would, moreover, be in conformity with the Commission's interpretation in its General Comment No. 4 on the Charter concerning the right to redress for victims of torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment.

In that general comment, the Commission emphasized that one of the measures States must take to combat impunity for the violence committed would be to "establish effective and clear instructions for public officials, including law enforcement officials as well as defence and security forces, and provide them with continuous training on the obligations of States Parties under the African Charter, notably with regard to the absolute prohibition of torture and the specific needs of marginalized, disadvantaged and discriminated populations".
It follows that the Complainants' request is suitable. f. On the recommendation of the establishment of awareness-raising and communication strategies

The Complainants also request the Commission to require the Respondent State to put in place awareness-raising, education and communication strategies vis-à-vis the population in general, and security agents and magistrates in particular, with a view to the eradication of torture and sexual violence in the DRC.

The Commission finds this request superfluous, because it considers that other recommendations already issued, notably that of the human rights module, suffice to educate key persons who can contribute to the eradication of torture and sexual violence e. On the presentation of public apologies to the victims

The Complainants implore the Commission to recommend that the Respondent State present public apologies to the victims within six months following the notification of the decision. According to them, in this procedure, the State should consult with the victims or their representatives on the modalities of the apologies, such as the place and date of their holding. The said apologies should be broadcast through the media.

The notion of public apologies is not new in matters of reparations for human rights violations. Thus, for example, in the case of Kichwa Indigenous People of Sarayaku v. Ecuador, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requested the State to make a public acknowledgment of international responsibility in respect of the violations that the court had found in the judgment. Likewise, in its general comment No. 4 concerning the right to redress for victims of torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment (Article 5); the Commission recognizes that satisfaction as a mode of reparation may include public apologies, including acknowledgment of the facts and acceptance of responsibility.
It follows that the Complainants' request is suitable and recommendable

The Complainants also pray the Commission to require the Respondent State to construct a monument bearing the names of all the victims, in a public space in the administrative headquarters of Fizi territory, within a period of one year following the notification of the judgment.

In the Ogiek case, the African Court considered that the commemoration of victims of human rights violations by the erection of a memorial is a recognized form of reparation in international law because it essentially enables the honouring of the victims and the recalling of the violations that were committed in the hope that this will contribute to preventing their recurrence. However, it noted that, considering the circumstances of the case, notably the measures it had ordered, it was not necessary to erect a monument.

Likewise, in the present case, the Commission considers that the erection of a monument on which the names of the victims would be inscribed is not necessary. Indeed, the Commission notes in the Complainants' submissions that the victims are stigmatized in society and consequently pointed at. An inscription of their names in a public place risks reinforcing this feeling of stigmatization. Moreover, the victims of the acts perpetrated by the soldiers are still alive. In this sense, the Commission considers that it would be aberrant to erect a monument commemorating the violations of the rights of the victims during their lifetime.

The Complainants request that the Respondent State publish at its own expense the decision on the merits in an official government gazette within six months following the notification of the decision.

The publication of a judicial decision is a procedure known in the human rights protection system in matters of reparation. In particular, the Inter-American Court has considered in numerous decisions that the publication of a judicial decision is an important measure of satisfaction for the victims of human rights violations. Thus, for example, in the case between the Xákmok Kásek Indigenous Community v. Paraguay, the Court required the Republic of Paraguay to publish certain parts of its judgment in an official gazette, the publication of a summary of the judgment prepared by the same court in a daily newspaper of national scope and the publication of the judgment in its entirety on an official government website for a period of at least one year.
It follows that this request of the Complainants is suitable and acceptable
The Complainants implore the Commission to take any other measure it might deem necessary in the interest of justice for the victims.
The Commission considers that it would be good for the Respondent State to report to the Commission within 180 days on the measures undertaken to implement the Commission's recommendations.

Declares that: i. Articles 1, 5, 6, 7, 14 and 16 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights were violated; ii. Articles 3(1), 4(1), 16, and 19(c) of the Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Women in Africa were violated; iii. 8(a) & (e) and 14(1) of the Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Women in Africa were not violated.

Consequently, the Commission requests the Democratic Republic of the Congo to: a) prosecute and punish the perpetrators of the violations within six months from the notification of the decision on the merits, and ensure the immediate enforcement of the judgment of the High Military Court once rendered. The enforcement shall be carried out without prejudice to subsequent recommendations issued by the African Commission. b) identify the real victims of the abuses committed by the soldiers in the present case in order to grant them the necessary monetary reparation in accordance with national procedures c) offer free and immediate, adequate and effective medical and psychological or psychiatric support, through specialized public health institutions to the victims who request it. d) include a module on human rights with a particular emphasis on women's rights in the training curriculum of soldiers, magistrates and other law enforcement officers. e) present public apologies to the victims within six months following the notification of the decision in a public event widely broadcast on the airwaves of a covering the region of the victims f) publish at its own expense the decision on the merits in an official government gazette within six months following the notification of the decision. g) report to it in writing, within one hundred and eighty (180) days of the notification of the present decision, on the measures undertaken for the implementation of these recommendations. Adopted by the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights at its 74th Ordinary Session held virtually from 21 February 2023 to 7 March 2023.

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights received a Complaint on 19 October 2022 from the African Human Rights Club and Ndukwe Charles Ndukwe on behalf of Maryam Aslyed Tiyrab against the Republic of the Sudan (the Respondent State).

The Complainants allege that on 26 June 2022, a 20-year-old girl named Maryam Alsyed Tiyrab was sentenced to death by stoning by the Kotsi Criminal Court in White Nile State, Sudan, due to her conviction for violating Article 146 (2) of the Sudanese Penal Code of 1991, which pertains to adultery.

The Complainants submit that the judicial decision mentioned above constitutes a severe violation of several international human rights instruments to which Sudan is a state party, such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the UN Convention against Torture (CAT), and the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter), which explicitly safeguard the right to life and prohibit torture, cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment or punishments.

The Complainants allege that the principle of fair hearing was violated in Maryam Alsyed Tiyrab's trial, due to the fact that she was interrogated by the police without being informed that the information she disclosed would be used as evidence against her in a criminal trial, which is contrary to the Sudanese Penal Code. Additionally, the Complainants state that her trial began without a formal complaint from the police in Kotsi, contrary to the provisions of the Penal Code. They further allege that in violation of Article 135 (3) of the Penal Code, Maryam was denied legal representation before and during her trial.

The Complainants assert that the trial of Maryam Alsyed Tiyrab violated the international law principle of equality before the law and non-discrimination based on gender, as it specifically targeted women. They add that the Sudanese law on adultery is not only unnecessary and criminalizing but also discriminatory by singling out women while disregarding men.
The Complainants allege that the trial and verdict in the case of Maryam Alsyed Tiyrab constitute clear and explicit violations of Articles 2, 3, 5, and 7 of the African Charter.

The Complainants allege the violation of Articles 2, 4, 5, and 7 of the Charter, as well the corresponding provisions of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and UN Convention against torture.

The Complainants request the Commission to: i. Find violation of Articles 2, 4, 5, and 7 of the Charter, as well the corresponding provisions of the International Covenant on civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and UN Convention against torture (UNCAT); ii. Orders the suspension of the execution of the Complainant's death sentence until the Commission’s final decision on the case.
The Secretariat received the Complaint on 19 October 2022, and seized it on 31 October 2022. On the same day, Provisional Measures were granted.

On 30 May 2023, the Complainants informed the Commission via email that the Higher Court of the Republic of the Sudan had reversed the judgment of the Lower Court, which had initially sentenced the victim to death. The Higher Court ordered a retrial, and as a result, the Complainants requested the Commission to suspend the proceedings until the retrial is finalized.

On 14 June 2023, the Secretariat notified the Complainants that the reversing of the sentence by the Higher Court does not suspend the processing of their Compliant which is pending before the Commission.
On 12 June 2023, the Complainants notified the Commission via email about their decision to withdraw the Complaint.
On 4 July 2023, the Secretariat acknowledged the receipt of the email and informed both Parties that the decision to withdraw the Communication would be submitted for the Commission's consideration.

In the email sent to the Commission, the Complainants submitted that the Higher Court of the Republic of Sudan, on 22 November 2022, overturned the verdict of the Lower Court that had sentenced Maryam Aslyed Tiyrab to death by stoning due to a lack of fair hearing, subsequently ordering a retrial. Consequently, they decided to withdraw the Communication and await the complete outcome of the Victim's pursuit of local remedies.

The Commission acknowledges the Complainants' request to withdraw the Communication, which is based on the fact that the Higher Court of the Respondent State has reversed the judgment of the lower court that sentenced the victim to death and has ordered a retrial.
From the above, the Commission sees no objection in granting this request.
The Commission decides to grant the request for withdrawal.

Based on the above the Commission declares the Communication Closed. Adopted at the seventy-sixth (76) Private Ordinary Session of the African Commission held virtually, from 19 July to 2 August 2023.

Le Secrétariat de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (le Secrétariat) a reçu le 10 novembre 2015, une Communication introduite en vertu de l'article 55 de la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Charte africaine) par Maître Lambert Nigarura ci-après dénommé le Plaignant, pour le compte de la Radio Publique Africaine ci-après dénommée la R.P.A ou la victime contre la République du Burundi ci-après dénommée le Burundi ou État défendeur.

Le Plaignant rapporte que la R.P.A est victime de son travail d'investigation qui ne plaît pas au pouvoir en place au Burundi. Il indique que le pouvoir Burundais n'a pas apprécié la retransmission par la R.P.A d'un élément sonore qui faisait la lumière sur l'assassinat de trois (3) sœurs religieuses en date du 8 septembre 2014 et qu'en plus de cela, la retransmission en directe des manifestations contre la troisième candidature du Président Pierre Nkurunziza par la R.P.A est venue aggraver la situation. Il argue que le pouvoir a décidé d'user de n'importe quel moyen pour faire définitivement taire la R.P.A.

Le Plaignant rapporte que le 26 avril 2015, au premier jour des manifestations retransmises en direct sur les ondes de la R.P.A et avec d'autres radio locales indépendantes, la R.P.A a reçu la visite de trois ministres à savoir le Ministre de l'Intérieur, le Ministre de la Sécurité publique et le Ministre de la Communication. Il précise que ces autorités ont intimé la rédaction de la R.P.A de suspendre la retransmission du déroulement des manifestations.

Le Plaignant indique qu'en date du 27 avril 2015, la Radio Télévision Nationale du Burundi a selon lui, en violation flagrante de la convention qui la lie aux radios privées, coupé les émetteurs qui permettaient la diffusion des émissions privées à l'intérieur du pays. Le Plaignant ajoute que deux jours plus tard, un contingent de la police et certains membres du service de renseignement ont envahi pour la seconde fois les locaux de la R.P.A, muni d'un mandat de fermeture provisoire de la Radio alors que selon le Plaignant, il n'appartenait pas au Ministère Public de se saisir d'office d'un délit de presse si délit il y avait; que depuis cette date, la R.P.A a été interdite d'émettre sur toute l'étendue du territoire Burundais et que la Direction de la Radio a malgré tout obtempéré sans résistance.

Le Plaignant rapporte en outre que le 13 mai 2015, un groupe de militaire qui a tenté de prendre le pouvoir par la force a envahi les locaux de la R.P.A pour exiger sa réouverture de force afin de faire passer leur message à la Nation. Le Plaignant précise que les agents de gardiennage seuls sur les lieux ont été obligés de donner les coordonnées des journalistes ; que les putschistes sont allés chercher les journalistes à leurs domiciles et les ont forcés à ouvrir la radio pour faire passer leur message.

Selon le Plaignant, cette réouverture forcée par les putschistes a conduit le pouvoir à mettre en exécution son projet d'en découdre définitivement avec la R.P.A et que c'est ainsi que, dans la matinée du 14 mai 2015, lors de l'échec du putsch, les forces loyalistes ont attaqué à la roquette les locaux de la R.P.A, l'ont détruite et l'ont incendiée. Le Plaignant ajoute que depuis ce jour, la chasse de tous les journalistes de la R.P.A a commencé et que ces derniers sont désormais éparpillés dans les pays voisins.

Le Plaignant estime que la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Commission) devrait l'exonérer de l'application de la condition de l'épuisement des voies de recours internes. A ce propos, il soutient d'une part, que la saisine des juridictions Burundaises serait vaine du fait qu'elles ne sont pas indépendantes et que considérant la R.P.A comme une « caisse résonante des putschistes », le Gouvernement Burundais n'a pas la volonté et la capacité de traiter ce dossier. D'autre part, le Plaignant soutient qu'il est dangereux d'utiliser les voies de recours internes car depuis la destruction de la R.P.A, tout le personnel de la R.P.A vit dans la clandestinité totale, que les journalistes sont pourchassés, que le Directeur de la R.P.A est recherché par la justice Burundaise et l'avocat de la R.P.A a lui-même été cité dans le rapport d'enquête judiciaire du seul fait qu'il se soit prononcé contre la troisième candidature du Président Pierre Nkurunziza.
Le Plaignant soutient que les droits de la R.P.A ont été violés mais que le peuple Burundais a par la même voie été privé de son droit à l'information et du droit de diffuser ses opinions.

Le Plaignant estime que la Commission exige désormais que les plaintes devant elle soient introduites dans un délai de six mois suivant l'épuisement des voies de recours internes ou la date retenue par la Commission ; il rappelle qu'en l'espèce, il y a lieu de le dispenser de l'épuisement des voies de recours internes et que les derniers faits datent du 14 mai 2015.
Le Plaignant indique en outre qu'aucun autre mécanisme de règlement international de différend n'a été saisi du cas d'espèce pour une quelconque analyse.
Le Plaignant n'a pas indiqué qu'il requiert l'anonymat.
A l'examen des moyens invoqués par le Plaignant, ce dernier allègue essentiellement la violation des dispositions des articles 1, 7(1), 9(1) et (2), 10, 12(2), 13, 14 et 26 de la Charte africaine.

Le Plaignant demande à la Commission : • d'user de sa compétence prévue à l'article 30 de la Charte africaine afin que la R.P.A recouvre ses droits transgressés et prévus par la Charte africaine (article 9), quant aux recommandations à intervenir qui seront intimées au Burundi ; • de condamner l'État défendeur afin qu'il indemnise illico la Radio Publique Africaine détruite selon lui injustement et illégalement ; • de constater avec lui que si un État partie ne peut pas assurer le respect des droits contenus dans la Charte africaine, ceci constitue une violation de ladite Charte et qu'en conséquence il apparaît que la législation de l'État défendeur ne respecte pas à cet égard, les engagements conventionnels du pays découlant du statut d'État partie à la Charte africaine.
Le Secrétariat de la Commission africaine a reçu la Communication le 10 novembre 2015.

Le Secrétariat, par lettre du 3 décembre 2015, a demandé au Plaignant de fournir certaines clarifications et pièces manquantes. Le Secrétariat a précisément demandé au Plaignant d'indiquer la raison pour laquelle sa Communication porte à titre liminaire deux références, d'indiquer quelles sont les victimes exactes dans le cas d'espèce et s'il est habilité à agir en leur nom et pour leur compte et enfin de fournir une pièce citée dans le contenu de la plainte mais qui n'a pas été transmise au Secrétariat.
Par correspondances des 7 et 9 décembre 2015, le Plaignant a fourni l'information et les clarifications requises ; le Secrétariat en a accusé réception par lettre du 18 décembre 2015.
Lors de sa 19 Session extraordinaire tenue à Banjul en Gambie du 16 au 25 février 2016, la Commission a examiné la Plainte et a décidé de s'en saisir.

Le 8 mars 2016, le Secrétariat a informé le Plaignant et l'État défendeur de cette décision et a demandé au Plaignant de soumettre ses observations sur la Recevabilité dans un délai de deux mois, conformément à l'article 105 (1) du règlement intérieur de la Commission.

Lors de sa 58 Session ordinaire tenue du 6 au 20 avril 2016 à Banjul, en Gambie, la Commission a examiné la Communication et a décidé de renvoyer sa décision sur la recevabilité en vue d'attendre les soumissions des parties. Le 28 avril 2016, les Parties ont été informées de cette décision l'une par lettre et l'autre par note verbale.

Le 2 mai 2016, le Plaignant a soumis au Secrétariat son mémoire sur la Recevabilité en indiquant que la version physique du dossier contenant d'autres éléments de preuves lui sera transmise par courrier postal.
Par lettre du 13 mai 2016, le Secrétariat en a accusé réception et a indiqué au Plaignant qu'il restait en attente du dossier physique qu'il avait mentionné.
Le 11 mai 2016, le Secrétariat a reçu le dossier physique et en a accusé réception par lettre du 17 mai 2016 tout en indiquant au Plaignant que l'annexe numéro 2 mentionnée n'y figure pas.

Par courriel du 20 mai 2016, le Plaignant a indiqué que la mention de l'annexe numéro 2 dans le dossier était un laspus calami et a ajouté que le contenu de ladite annexe se trouve en fait dans le CD joint au dossier. Le Secrétariat a accusé réception de ce courriel le 20 mai 2016.

Le 30 mai 2016, le Secrétariat a transmis le mémoire du Plaignant sur la Recevabilité à l'État défendeur et a invité ce dernier à soumettre ses observations dans un délai de deux mois conformément à l'article 105 (2) du Règlement intérieur de la Commission.

Le 19 juillet 2016, le Secrétariat a informé le Plaignant et l'État défendeur que l'audience sollicitée par le Plaignant ne pourrait lui être accordée vu l'étape de l'examen de la Communication. Par ailleurs, la Commission a informé les Parties que la décision sur la Recevabilité est renvoyée à une Session ultérieure dans l'attente des observations de l'État défendeur.

Le 23 novembre 2016, le Secrétariat a informé l'État défendeur que la Commission a décidé de lui octroyer trente jours (30) calendaires supplémentaires pour la soumission de ses observations sur la Recevabilité. Le Plaignant a été informé de cette décision le même jour par lettre datée.
Jusqu-là, l'État défendeur n'a pas transmis ses observations sur la Recevabilité de la Communication malgré les nombreuses relances à lui faites.
Les 13 avril, 5 juin, 22 août et 8 décembre 2017, le Secrétariat a informé les Parties que la Commission a décidé de rendre sa décision sur la Recevabilité à une Session ultérieure.

Lors de sa 63 session ordinaire, tenue du 24 octobre au 13 novembre 2018, la Commission a déclaré la Communication recevable. Cette décision a été transmise aux Parties et le Plaignant a été invité à soumettre ses observations écrites sur le fond.
Le 10 septembre 2019, le plaignant a présenté ses observations sur le fond, qui ont été transmises à l'État défendeur le 7 janvier 2020, avec information au plaignant à la même date.

Le 16 mars 2020, le Secrétariat a rappelé à l'État défendeur que le délai qui lui était imparti pour présenter des observations sur le fond expirerait le 7 avril 2020 et que lors de la 27 session extraordinaire, l'examen de la communication a été reporté faute desdites observations.

En marge de la 73 session ordinaire, qui s'est tenue du 21 octobre au 10 novembre 2022, un fonctionnaire du Secrétariat a rencontré une délégation du Burundi pour discuter de l'état des affaires pendantes contre le Burundi. La délégation burundaise a été informée de la situation concernant les communications pendantes contre le Burundi.

Par note verbale Réf : ACHPR/1068/2022, datée du 31 novembre 2022, ladite Liste de Communications a ensuite été transmise à l'Ambassade du Burundi à Addis, Éthiopie le 3 novembre 2022, à la connaissance du Ministère de la Justice du Burundi. La liste a été partagée avec la délégation burundaise par courrier électronique le 7 novembre 2022. Cette communication fait partie des communications dans lesquelles l'État défendeur n'a pas soumis d'observations sur le fond.

Malgré l'envoi de la liste contenant l'état des communications en attente devant la Commission à l'encontre de l'État défendeur, y compris l'état de la présente communication, l'État défendeur n'a pas daigné présenter une demande de prorogation du délai ni soumettre ses observations sur le fond.
Le Plaignant fait valoir que la Communication respecte l'ensemble des conditions de recevabilité posées par l'article 56 de la Charte africaine.

L'identité de l'auteur de la Communication est indiquée conformément à l'article 56 (1) de la Charte. La Communication ayant été présentée par Maître Lambert Nigarura au nom de la Radio Publique Africaine dont les adresses et les coordonnées de contact sont bien précisées dans les soumissions.

Le Plaignant soutient que la Communication est compatible avec la Charte de l'OUA/UA ou avec la Charte africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples en vertu de l'article 56 (2) de la Charte. Aux dires du Plaignant, la présente Communication est dirigée contre la République du Burundi, un État partie à la Charte depuis le 28 juillet 1989. Les violations alléguées dans la Communication enfreignent les droits garantis par les articles 1, 7(1), 9(1) et (2), 10, 12(2), 13, 14 et 26 de la Charte africaine.
Lesdites violations sont postérieures à la ratification de la Charte par l'État défendeur.
Le Plaignant affirme que la Communication est dépourvue de tout langage insultant vis-à-vis de l'État mis en cause, ses institutions ou de l'OUA conformément à l'article 56 (3) de la Charte.

Le Plaignant déclare que la Communication n'est pas basée sur des nouvelles diffusées par des moyens de communication de masse en application de l'article 56 (4). L'annexe de la Communication contient en effet des éléments d'enquêtes élaborées conjointement par des représentants des trois pouvoirs : exécutif, législatif, judiciaire, des partenaires techniques et financiers et de la société civile.

Le Plaignant affirme que pour ce qui est de l'épuisement des voies de recours internes, selon la jurisprudence de la Commission dans la Communication 328/06 Frente de Libertação do Estado de Cabinda contra a República de Angola, 2013, paragraphe 44, le respect de cette exigence doit reposer sur trois critères à savoir que le recours doit être : disponible, efficace et suffisant. Le Plaignant ajoute que tel qu'il résulte de la décision de la Commission dans la Communication 409/12 Luke Munyandu Tembani et autres contre l'Angola, la règle de l'épuisement des recours internes ne s'applique pas si les recours n'existent pas, s'ils se prolongent de façon indue ou s'ils sont rendus impossibles. Le Plaignant soutient que les voies de recours sont inexistantes car ni lui, ni la victime ou encore les, représentants de la Radio Publique Africaine ne pouvaient se rendre devant les tribunaux sans s'inquiéter ou encore sans mettre en danger leur intégrité physique et psychologique.

Le Plaignant énonce également que les voies de recours sont rendues indisponibles en tant que l'appareil judiciaire serait aux mains de l'exécutif. Il estime que la Commission devrait le dispenser de la condition d'épuisement des voies de recours qui n'offrent aucune chance de succès conformément à la jurisprudence de la Commission, dans l'affaire Dawda K. Jawara c. Gambie, qui considère que la condition de l'épuisement des recours internes ne s'applique pas lorsque ces recours « ne sont pas disponibles ou sont inefficaces. Le Plaignant mentionne qu'il pourrait donc être dispensé du respect de cette exigence en raison du manque d'indépendance du système judiciaire burundais soumis au contrôle de l'exécutif ainsi que des craintes de persécution des personnes physiques représentantes du Plaignant.

Le Plaignant rappelle que la condition imposée au paragraphe 6 de l'article 56 de la Charte africaine concernant le délai raisonnable repose sur deux possibilités : introduction de la Communication dans un délai raisonnable courant depuis l'épuisement des recours internes ou depuis la date retenue par la Commission comme faisant commencer à courir le délai de sa propre saisine. Le Plaignant estime que dans le cas d'espèce, étant donné qu'il n'a pas épuisé les voies de recours, la question du délai ne saurait courir. Il s'en remet donc à l'appréciation de la Commission.

Le Plaignant déclare enfin que la Communication ne concerne pas des cas qui ont été réglés par une autre instance internationale en application de l'article 56(7) de la charte. Selon le Plaignant, les allégations contenues dans cette communication n'ont été portées devant aucun autre organe régional, continental ou international. Ceci étant, il prétend que cette condition ne souffre d'aucune insuffisance.

L'État défendeur n'a pas soumis ses observations sur la Recevabilité en dépit des multiples Notes Verbales de rappel que le Secrétariat lui a adressé à cet effet; notamment les Notes verbale suivantes : ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/378/16, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/1052/16, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/1372/16, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/1875/16, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/264/17, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/396/17, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/688/17, et ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/1580/17 respectivement du 8 mars 2016, 30 mai 2016, 19 juillet 2016, 23 novembre 2016, 13 avril 2017, 5 juin 2017, 22 août 2017 et 8 décembre 2017.

La Communication a été introduite sur le fondement de l'article 55 de la Charte africaine qui donne compétence à la Commission pour recevoir et examiner les « communications autres que celles émanant des États parties ». Lesdites communications doivent, pour être déclarées recevables, remplir les conditions prévues à l'article 56 de la Charte africaine.

Aux termes des dispositions de l'article 105(2) de son Règlement intérieur de 2010, le Secrétariat transmet à l'État défendeur, les moyens soumis par le Plaignant pour répondre. En l'espèce, la Commission note que les prescriptions procédurales ainsi rappelées ont été observées tel qu'en attestent les nombreuses Notes Verbales rappelant à l'État défendeur de transmettre ses observations sur la Recevabilité. Sur la base de ces constatations, la Commission décide d'examiner la Communication sur la base des éléments en sa possession, conformément à sa pratique.

Cette question de procédure réglée, la Commission va se pencher sur la Recevabilité proprement dite de la Communication sous examen. Sur le point du respect de la condition posée à l'article 56(1) de la Charte africaine, la Commission note que la Communication identifie clairement le Plaignant et la victime représentée dont les coordonnées et adresses complètes ont été fournies dans les soumissions déposées devant elle. La Commission estime que la Communication respecte par conséquent la condition examinée.

Pour ce qui concerne le respect des dispositions de l'article 56(2) de la Charte africaine, la Commission rappelle que l'exigence posée s'entend de la compatibilité ratione personae, ratione materiae, ratione temporis et ratione loci de la Communication avec l'Acte Constitutif de l'Union Africaine et la Charte africaine. Ainsi, l'examen de compatibilité doit consister pour la Commission à s'assurer que tous les moyens et demandes contenus dans la Communication sont conformes aux dispositions des instruments ci-dessus cités.

La Commission note qu'en l'espèce, la Communication est introduite contre la République du Burundi, État partie à la Charte africaine depuis le 28/07/1989 et que le Plaignant a qualité pour agir. En outre, le Plaignant allègue la violation, sur le territoire de l'État défendeur, de droits protégés par la Charte, notamment la violation des articles 1, 7(1), 9(1) et (2), 10, 12(2), 13, 14 et 26. La Commission note par ailleurs que la Charte était en vigueur au Burundi à l'époque des faits. Enfin, il est manifeste que ni les moyens ni les demandes contenues dans la Communication n'enfreignent aucun des principes adoptés aux termes de l'Acte Constitutif de l'Union Africaine. En conséquence, la Commission conclut que la Communication respecte les dispositions de l'article 56(2) de la Charte africaine.

Sur le respect des dispositions de l'article 56(3), la Commission note que la Communication ne contient aucun terme susceptible d'être qualifié d'insultant ou outrageant à l'égard de l'État défendeur, de ses institutions ou de l'Union Africaine. La Communication remplit par conséquent la condition sous examen.

La Commission note également que l'exigence faite à l'article 56(4) est respectée puisque la Communication contient en annexe, entre autres, un document officiel produit conjointement par les institutions de l'État défendeur dont les représentants du gouvernement, du pouvoir législatif, du pouvoir judiciaire, des partenaires techniques et financiers ainsi que des membres la société civile.

Sur le point du respect par la Communication de la condition d'épuisement des voies de recours internes aux termes de l'article 56(5) de la Charte africaine, la Commission dans sa pratique procède à l'examen, l'une après l'autre, des violations supposées violées.

Dans la pratique jurisprudentielle de la Commission, l'objectif de la condition contenue à l'article 56 (5) de la Charte africaine est de permettre à l'État mis en cause en l'occurrence le Burundi de régler en priorité, selon son droit interne, la violation des droits de l'homme alléguée avant son examen par une instance internationale, pour éviter qu'une telle instance ne soit utilisée comme un tribunal de première instance mais plutôt qu'elle soit un organe de dernier recours.

Dans le cas d'espèce, l'auteur de la Communication n'a introduit aucune requête devant les tribunaux internes de l'État burundais, admettant que les voies de recours internes n'offrent aucune chance de succès. Le Plaignant soutient que le contrôle que le gouvernement exerce sur le pouvoir judiciaire est de nature à ne pas rendre indépendante l'institution et en tant que tel, les chances d'aboutissement des saisines dans le cadre de cette affaire sont très minces, ce qui rendrait les recours internes inefficaces et non satisfaisants.

Dans sa décision de principe en la matière, la Commission précise le sens des dispositions de l'article 56(5) en décidant dans l'affaire Dawda K. Jawara c. Gambie que les recours à épuiser doivent être disponibles, efficaces et satisfaisants.
